p+Pb dataset at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 8.5$ TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 25 nb$^{-1}$ for each beam target. This data has been examined across multiple channels to investigate the influence of neutral lead fragments on the production of Higgs bosons and other heavy particles in mixed nucleon-target collisions. An analysis of di-photon and $\mu^+\mu^+$ final states in both p+Pb and pb+Pb reactions reveals consistent findings: Higgs production in p+Pb exhibits a central rapidity distribution that is broader than in pp collisions, with both tails displaced toward the fragment end. Furthermore, the total cross section in p+Pb is estimated to be 1.3 to 2.1 times larger than in pp, depending on the rapidity region examined. In contrast, the total Higgs production cross section in pb+Pb shows no significant deviation from the pp result. Additionally, the transverse momentum of Higgs bosons in p+Pb is found to be smaller than in pp collisions. These observations align with predictions from models attributing the effects to neutral hadrons produced within the target nucleus. The data further support previous findings indicating that bottom quark production in p+Pb possesses a broader rapidity profile and lower transverse momentum compared to pp collisions. Finally, the studies confirm the absence of charm quark production within neutral fragments and place constraints on the properties of neutral hadrons generated inside the proton-nucleus target. The results from the Higgs analysis are consistent with recent observations of a broader rapidity distribution and enhanced total cross section for $D^{*}D^{*}$ production in p+Pb relative to pp collisions. However, previous reports of an enhanced total cross section for $J/\psi J/\psi$ production in p+Pb are not reproduced in this study. These findings offer constraints on interpretations of the total cross-section enhancement in lead-lead collisions at LHC energies. Published in Physical Review Letters.

The system utilizes a simple outer LDPC code with a (64800, 51840, 16) configuration, a 100 GHz optically spaced WDM structure, and 50 GHz-channelized chromatic dispersion compensation. Achieved bit error rate (BER) floors of less than $3.8 \times 10^{-9}$ in field trials confirm the theoretical potential of 4.3 Gbit/s OOK links, which feature an ultra-simple hardware configuration and low-cost, mass-produced components. Notably, the (64800, 51840, 16) LDPC code was selected for its ability to maximize the number of optical channels while maintaining a feasible BER floor, a feature that was validated both theoretically and experimentally. With optical amplifiers and chromatic dispersion compensators spaced at 80 km intervals, the system exhibits remarkable robustness against dispersion-induced nonlinearities, requiring only a factor-of-1.07 increase in optimum input power per 100 km of uncompensated dispersion. This research provides the first theoretical and experimental justification that short-reach optimized hardware can be directly applied to transoceanic distances with suitable optimization. Consequently, this field-trial design serves as an effective reference for optimizing both single-wavelength single-bit/symbol (SB/S) and multi-wavelength multi-bit/symbol (SB/S) optical links. Since its theoretical throughputs approach the maximum feasible rates, this system demonstrates that the energy per bit to noise power spectral density ratio ($E_{\rm b}/N_0$) required for a target BER can serve as a reliable metric for estimating the maximum transmission distance in both SB/S and SD/S optical communication. We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Furthermore, our method generates a diverse collection of Pareto-optimal TCNs from a single initial model, surpassing manually designed solutions in both efficiency and performance. Benefiting from compatibility with existing learning rate aware dilation factor estimators, our framework is broadly applicable. Experiments across various models and datasets—including the UCR time series benchmark and CMU human activity recognition—demonstrate consistent advantages over current state-of-the-art methods. The implementation is openly available at https://github.com/zhuhan2344/AutoDilated.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel at high accuracy for static image classification, adapting them to dynamic, multivariate time-series data remains difficult due to the adverse impact of noise and limited training samples. We present the first Continuous Valuation Network (CVN), which utilizes sweep line convolutions and nonlinear smoothing to convert multi-dimensional time series into meaningful scalar estimates of value and trend. This transformation allows standard CNN classifiers to achieve state-of-the-art performance, particularly in low-data regimes. The model is computationally lightweight, easily integrated into modern AI accelerators, and is released under the open-source license at https://github.com/robertgeusk/CVN.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are a dominant class of deep learning models used for classifying time series, but they depend on carefully crafted architectures and extensive data. We propose the First Order Neural Network (FONN), a minimal model based on first-order differential equations that processes time series by aggregating observations through a matrix exponential. Fonn offers a compact, interpretable, and efficient solution that delivers competitive accuracy. By treating the series as a trajectory and leveraging the smoothness of exponential functions, FONN effectively learns the underlying dynamics. It supports extracting both class-probability outputs and implicit feature representations at any point in time. Evaluation on two benchmarks shows that FONN matches the accuracy of complex CNNs while using 76x fewer parameters, and it outperforms other lightweight

We define the correction of a table as producing two sets of corrected rows: one positive instance set to fill the missing values and one negative instance set representing the null values. We establish the feasibility of approximating table completion as a satisfaction problem and provide polynomial-time algorithms to convert instances of 3-SAT into table completion problems, enabling the filling of missing values while respecting a given subset of functional dependencies. Furthermore, we define constraints on positive and negative instances to induce four types of non-relational functional dependencies. We demonstrate that most of these dependencies rely on having no missing values. Additionally, we introduce a method for inducing a non-relational functional dependency by a table with missing values, showing that its correction is feasible and that its positive instance set can be converted into a relational functional dependency. Finally, we outline criteria for determining the cost of correcting a table and define the associated optimization problem. This paper is a revised and expanded version of the paper presented at ICCL 2020.

We show that while this problem is generally coNP-complete, it becomes NP-complete (and tractable) under specific conditions. a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for 3D pose. Because descriptors are translation-equivariant, the optimization landscape allows for efficient exploration across a broad range of initial poses. In demonstrations, we achieve accurate pose estimation on unseen objects with a mean pose error of under $7cm$ on a challenging instance, a result that requires no training after the single demonstration. Furthermore, we demonstrate how a few supervised adjustments can further refine the estimated poses. To our knowledge, this is the first method capable of estimating the 3D poses of unseen object instances from a single demonstration. By decoupling the representation from specific 3D poses, NDFs offer a new perspective for tasks in robot demonstration and transfer learning. We present Instance Neural Fields (INFs), a solution for instance segmentation within a object's point cloud that does not rely on global features. Unlike recent methods that encode both object and camera coordinates to generate global point descriptors for instance pooling, INFs employ a recursive nearest neighbor strategy. This allows the model to segment an object by encoding only local neighborhoods, recursively re-encoding and classifying the nearest unclassified points to progressively build the instance mask. This technique, akin to point-based message passing or point neural fields, is particularly beneficial for instance segmentation, as it minimization inter-instance interference by focusing on local encoding rather than global space partitioning. Additionally, this method is advantageous for real-time applications, as it reduces the amount of data passed to downstream classifiers. We validate our approach on the SUN RGB-D and indoor scenes from the Shape Networks datasets. Our method outperforms recent competitive techniques, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) of $47.0$ for the largest instance, which corresponds to a specific instance area of approximately $0.37m^2$. Source code is available at https://github.com/Stanford-VMG/Instance_Neural_Fields.

for the future International Linear Collider (ILC), a configuration validated in 2012. It employs a compact, cost-effective architecture tailored for precise Higgs boson measurements and sensitivity to diverse new physics phenomena. By integrating a robust silicon vertex and tracking system with a five Tesla central solenoidal magnet, the design achieves superior momentum resolution. Additionally, its highly granular calorimeter is optimized for Particle Flow techniques, ensuring excellent jet energy resolution across a broad energy spectrum. As the ILC's potential construction date approaches, it is crucial to review the design and technology decisions finalized during the Design-Building (DBD) phase, updating them based on recent technological advancements. ofs has expanded substantially, forming a vast repository of research that offers numerous opportunities for statistical analysis across various facets of theorem proving, though these potential applications remain largely untapped. Yet, this expansion introduces specific challenges, as locating materials becomes progressively more difficult while the need for reusability and clarity grows. This thesis abstract outlines my research agenda focused on these issues and briefly highlights preliminary findings suggesting that the dependency graph of the archive exhibits a scale-free distribution in terms of node in-degree. Furthermore, we contend that the archive displays clear structural organization, with many components clusterable by functional categories such as "tools," "logics," or "applications." Finally, the study explores methods for enhancing the discoverability of papers and library entries within the archive, potentially leveraging their often rich metadata. This work was conducted while the author was supported by an NSF GRFP, which also funded related preliminary studies.
The reliance of modern programming on type systems has been identified, and prior work has attempted to model these system properties, often representing them as forms of context-dependency similar to conditional type formations. This paper builds on that foundation to formally model multiple properties of dependently typed programming, specifically untyped (non-dependent) types, coinductive types, and type equality. It demonstrates that a logic capable of reasoning about these concepts must extend beyond standard first-order logic with equality.
The practice of formalizing multiple equivalent versions of the same theorem has numerous advantages, yet it remains unclear how to systematically measure their mathematical distance. This abstract briefly introduces the notion of a "commute diagram," a multifaceted structure that encapsulates the relationships between mathematically equivalent objects. This definition is significant as it represents a set of formal objects that can potentially serve as data points for statistical research within theorem proving. Additionally, the abstract defines a metric space to measure distances between these objects and sketches how an algorithm could compute such metrics.
In the pursuit of reusing library components, one must not only locate a suitable function but also verify that its dependencies are appropriate for the current context, a process that becomes increasingly complex as library sizes grow. Although researchers have attempted to assess the difficulty of finding functions, there has been limited effort in evaluating the complexity of making them work. This work presents methods for quantifying the context required for a function to operate, including both the size of the necessary context and its structural properties. These metrics facilitate the comparison of functions across a diverse range of contexts, revealing distinct patterns in how the complexity of made-workable code varies compared to discovery difficulty.

At a specific value of the coupling constant, the conformal field theory governing $N_f$ massless Dirac fermions coupled to a complex $U(N)$ gauge field becomes identical to that of $2N_f$ real scalar fields with global $U(N)$ symmetry. Field-theoretic arguments suggest that introducing a complex chemical potential for the fermions within the $U(N)$ symmetry group drives the system with $N_f$ fermions to volume non-analycity at the same critical density found in the corresponding $N$-vector model. Defined as intricate electromagnetic structures, they are characterized by extreme thinness relative to the wavelength, extensive transverse dimensions, and composition of subwavelength scatterers with minute features. These structures often exhibit properties such as bianisotropy, spatial and temporal variability, nonlinearity, curvature, and multiphysics interactions. Given this complexity, effective metasurface design demands a comprehensive strategy that integrates synergistic synthesis and analysis grounded in a robust theoretical model. The Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs), when paired with bianisotropic surface susceptibility, offer such a framework, enabling the creation of advanced metasurfaces through printing, etching, growth, or 3D fabrication. This paper addresses the often-overlooked challenge of inversely determining a metasurface's susceptibility from electromagnetic field measurements, specifically focusing on resolving ambiguities and enhancing accuracy in the presence of multipath interference. We propose a novel susceptibility extraction technique that avoids traditional matrix inversion methods, thereby eliminating issues related to structure thickness and curvature. Additionally, we introduce an innovative forward analysis approach for thick, curved, and multiphysics metasurfaces, validated through two case studies: a rotated cross-shaped metallic split-ring resonator and a curved nonlinear metasurface. These applications demonstrate the potential of GSTCs to simplify the design of thin, curved, and complex metasurfaces, significantly reducing the time and cost currently required for structure synthesis. Ultimately, this work paves the way for smart, self-tuned metasurfaces that can adaptively control wave propagation by adjusting their susceptibility in real-time based on external stimuli. This research is particularly crucial for multiphysics metasurfaces, which are essential for next-generation wireless systems, electromagnetic compatibility, energy harvesting, and super surfaces.

These functions effectively capture the intricate instantaneous spatial correlations between electrons in many-electron atoms. The eCPNN was trained unsupervised using limited Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) one-electron density data, adhering to predefined accuracy thresholds. By utilizing the effective correlation potential functions produced by the eCPNN, we can predict the total energies of the investigated atomic systems with exceptional precision relative to FCI energies. Introduction: In quantum chemistry, the FCI method is renowned for delivering benchmark accuracy by exactly solving the non-relativistic electronic Schrödinger equation within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. However, despite its accuracy, FCI is computationally prohibitive for all but the smallest molecules. To address this, reduced FCI approaches that truncate excited configurations have been widely employed; however, these methods still struggle to deliver the accuracy required for solving challenging problems in chemistry and physics. To date, no universal computational method exists that can solve molecular problems with both the high accuracy of FCI and the efficiency of mean-field theories like Hartree-Fock (HF) or Kohn-Sham (KS) density functional theory (DFT). Such a capability is essential for addressing numerous unresolved challenges, including accurately predicting chemical reactions, determining kinetic isotope effects, and calculating scalar relativistic effects. The most prevalent workaround involves employing FCI on small basis sets followed by post-FCI techniques like coupled cluster theory using larger basis sets. Nevertheless, this strategy is not ideal, as even fundamental properties like molecular dipoles can exhibit significant errors when combining FCI with smaller basis sets and coupled cluster methods with larger basis sets. The root cause of these issues lies in the fundamental approximation inherent in any fixed determinant method, such as HF or DFT: the assumption that the exact many-electron wavefunction can be adequately represented by a single Slater determinant

Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating correspondence learning with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We develop two GNN-based models, the Generalized Neural Correspondence Network (GNNcr) and the Sparse Neural Correspondence Network (Sparsecr), to directly learn 3D correspondences from intermediate cues across various pipelines. These frameworks are highly modular, requiring adjustments in only the first stage during training, while needing no modification in the second stage. Unlike traditional methods, our approach handles correspondence learning regardless of the nature of intermediate cues, the factorization of the 6D pose space, or the presence of occlusions. Evaluations on the Oxford Robot 6D (OX 6D) and TORDAR datasets demonstrate that our method enhances the performance of two existing pipelines by averaging 2.2° improvement in Average Degree of Freedom error (Avge°). Furthermore, experimental results indicate that our model effectively leverages the adjustability of parametric representations and excels in predicting poses for occluded objects. The code for our approach is available online.

We introduce a method to generate vortex structures within a binary black hole (BBH) system embedded in wave dark matter (WDM). These structures arise from the interference between the monopole distributions of the BBH and any pre-existing vortex configuration in the WDM. Our results indicate that as the BBHs migrate, these interference patterns can trigger the evolution of the vortex structure, potentially causing it to collapse as the components approach. Conversely, we observe that if the BBH is placed at a specific, larger separation, these interference patterns can disrupt the evolving vortex, preventing collapse. The success of this method in equal-mass systems suggests it can be applied to determine the initial setup for all BBH systems within WDM.

The edges are hinged at their outer vertices, while the central vertex allows for both translation and rotation; the rotational motion is influenced by a combination of elastic and frictional forces. We provide comprehensive findings regarding the asymptotic distribution and structure of the spectrum for the linear operator linked to the abstract spectral problem within a Hilbert space. As a supplementary result, we utilize the spectral analysis to establish the compactness of the operator's resolvent. This approach avoids the lengthy and technically demanding hypocoercivity arguments typically required for graphs or networks, offering explicit and direct proofs. Furthermore, the methods and insights derived throughout this paper are applicable to the stability analysis of solutions for the non-linear Cucker–Smallsdrift model. designed for causal discovery using observational data and domain-specific knowledge, focusing on causal graph and mechanism modeling. The 'cdt' package offers an end-to-end solution that recovers both the causal skeleton (direct dependencies) and the relationships between variables. It integrates algorithms from 'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg', alongside methods for pairwise causal discovery like ANM. The 'cdt' package is released under the MIT License and can be accessed at https://github.com/Diviyan-Kalainathan/CausalDiscoveryToolbox.

For modern machine learning systems, explaining outcomes is essential, particularly when incorporating domain knowledge. This work demonstrates how to integrate such knowledge into causal graph discovery from data. We propose a new algorithm, the Causal Taxonomy (CAT), which leverages domain expertise in the form of ordered attribute sets, potentially revealing hidden variables and their relationships. Implemented as the `cat` Python package, this method infers a causal graph respecting the given taxonomic structure, offering a more detailed and nuanced system than existing approaches. Initial tests on synthetic data and a Twitter spam detection dataset yield results comparable to current state-of-the-art single-tree methods (PC-LiNGAM) and the CAT package itself, confirming that domain knowledge can enhance both accuracy and the richness of discovered structures. The `cat` package is available at https://github.com/RichardEvans2/cat.

While previous methods often begin with a causal search among all variables to build a graph, high dimensionality and the curse of dimensionality make this difficult. A more scalable strategy is to define a high-dimensional marginal method and gradually assemble the full causal graph through conditioning, a process we term hierarchical causal discovery. However, reliable pairwise methods are scarce, and there has been a lack of frameworks to combine them with higher-dimensional techniques. Our `cat` package fills this gap, supporting various pairwise methods and facilitating hierarchical causal discovery.

We also present `cat` packages for both Python and R, which support generic pairwise causal discovery methods and enable the construction of causal graphs via a hierarchical approach. The theoretical foundations of `cat` are detailed in https://richardevans.sh/hierarchical-causal-discovery/.

By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. Additionally, we prove that the product of lattice spacing and the mass of the lightest charged state adheres to a scaling relation consistent with the conjecture. Ultimately, we propose a framework for examining global symmetry violations in various $\mathcal{N}=2$ four-dimensional effective field theories, suggesting that generalized $\theta$-terms, charged state spectra, and instanton corrections collectively ensure consistency. We further suggest that generalized $\theta$-terms serve as a novel characteristic of $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective theories, potentially indicating a generalized prepotential. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between generalized $\theta$-terms and anomalies associated with flavor symmetries in these frameworks. Finally, we offer a statement regarding the absence of flavor flavor anomalies arising from non-BPS states, which aligns with a recently introduced consistency condition.

Investigating robust reinforcement learning against adversarial corruption in both rewards and transitions is crucial, yet the impact of an adversary capable of arbitrarily modifying both signals remains insufficiently understood. We define such an adversary as one who can corrupt up to an $\epsilon$-fraction of episodes, with the capacity to adaptively corrupt specific steps in the remaining portions of these episodes. To cope with this setting, we present an algorithm with a guarantee of tolerance for an arbitrarily small $\epsilon$. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach can endure approximately an order of magnitude more corruption compared to prior algorithms, which are typically restricted to uncorrupted reward functions or transitions. Moreover, we establish both practical and theoretical bounds on performance, demonstrating that the practical guarantee is optimal. Consequently, this research significantly advances the state of the art by enhancing corruption tolerance by roughly an order of magnitude.

The box game, also referenced as the optimal strategy for a 1-D search, 1-D hidden number search, and the one-dimensional box problem, typically involves multiple players locating a hidden number $\xi$ within the interval $[0,1]$. In its standard configuration, players can ask questions, but each query that does not hit $\xi$ incurs a cost that constrains the total number of queries possible. The objective is often to determine the optimal strategy for estimating $\xi$. However, the results presented in this paper demonstrate that the box game can exhibit paradoxical behavior even when no queries are permitted. Specifically, we show that the players can correctly identify $\xi$ with a high probability despite having access to zero information about it.

Consider $N$ players, denoted by the index $i=1,2,\dots,N$, tasked with locating an unknown number $\xi$ drawn from a uniform distribution on the interval $[0,1]$. Unlike the standard version of the problem, the players are unable to pose any questions. Although they possess no information about $\xi$, 99 \% of the players can correctly identify $\xi$ using an estimator $\hat{\xi}(\xi)$ that does not infinitely diverge from $\xi$.

To achieve this counterintuitive outcome, the players employ a strategy that leverages the statistical properties of the uniform distribution of $\xi$. By utilizing a system of nested intervals and the fact that the probability of $\xi$ falling within any specific sub-interval can be calculated, the players can infer significant information about $\xi$'s location.

To estimate $\xi$, the players employ a strategy based on a Poisson point process. They imagine $M$ random integers, $j_1, j_2, \dots, j_M$, are drawn uniformly from the set $\{1, 2, \dots, N!\}$. The estimated value $\hat{\xi}(\xi)$ is then determined based on where $\xi$ would fall relative to these integers. This approach allows the players to effectively partition the interval $[0,1]$ into smaller segments and use the distribution of these integers to make an informed guess

While various models have been developed to describe multi-phonon effects, the Holstein model remains the most fundamental, representing superlattices where local Jahn-Teller effects are significant. To facilitate a comprehensive quantitative analysis of this system, we introduce a simplified Hamiltonian that retains key multi-phonon characteristics, including local Jahn-Teller phenomena, while excluding less critical parameters. Multi-phonon BEC holds substantial importance for understanding the electronic and lattice behaviors of heavy fermion materials, potentially aiding in the interpretation of experimental data regarding heavy fermion superconductivity.

We argue that this problem can be reframed as an image retrieval task, solvable through information gain or similar metrics. Furthermore, even within a professional setting, distinguishing between very high levels of semantic correctness and equivalence would be challenging for human annotators. Finally, Section 5 reviews related work and concludes the paper. In the Appendix, we provide additional details, including examples from each evaluation level, image sources, statistical analyses, and discussions on multi-modal evaluation and semantic image equivalence. We also clarify the distinctions between descriptive accuracy, semantic correctness, and semantic equivalence.

Machine translation systems routinely employ Translation Memory (TM) to leverage bilingual data. However, compiling TM from bilingual corpora is computationally prohibitive when dealing with large-scale resources, and the resulting index is difficult to utilize effectively. We propose using this translation memory outside of standard machine translation contexts. By translating sentences from a bilingual corpus into the target language and organizing them by source language identity, we can translate any source sentence that is similar—though not necessarily identical—to a paragraph in a monolingual corpus. Even without exact matches, we demonstrate that this paragraph-level TM substantially improves translation quality. Although the gain is modest, it scales effectively with corpus size. Our method is straightforward to implement and remains useful across various existing machine translation pipelines.

Translation Memory (TM) is widely recognized for boosting Machine Translation (MT) performance, typically by incorporating bilingual sentences into a retrievable index that shares subword vocabulary with the MT model. We present a novel approach that constructs TM solely from monolingual corpora, eliminating the need for a direct vocabulary overlap. This is achieved through cross-lingual embedding. Consequently, we can translate paragraphs within a monolingual corpus into the target language and utilize these translations as TM. Even when this memory is combined with a strong NMT model that has never seen this specific corpus, we observe significant gains in translation quality. This technique is particularly valuable for translating out-of-domain data, such as domain adaptation, and is particularly effective with larger corpus sizes. Our method is straightforward to implement and remains effective across different NMT models, including those based on attention and self-attention mechanisms that do not rely on vocabulary overlap. We also provide a complexity analysis for indexing monolingual TM and find that our method benefits significantly from increased corpus

**1 Introduction**

Traditional recommender systems often suffer from the cold-start and data sparsity challenges regarding new items and users. Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) emerges as a viable solution by leveraging information from related domains to improve recommendations within a primary target domain. Recently, interests migration-based CDR models have gained prominence by exploiting the similarity of user interests across related domains to enhance recommendation accuracy. However, most existing interests migration models operate on the premise that interests migrate from a single source domain to a single target domain, which often does not reflect the complexity of real-world user behavior.

First, users' interests are frequently fragmented across multiple domains; for instance, an e-commerce domain lacking sufficient data might benefit from user interest information in separate sport or book domains. Second, interests can migrate from a combined source domain, formed by merging multiple similar source domains, to a single target domain. Consequently, a more comprehensive and rigorous model is required to handle the migration of interests from multiple source domains to a single target domain, accounting for variations in the number and characteristics of these source domains.

By unifying volatile and nonvolatile memory, Persistent Memory (PM) has the potential to transform computing, potentially offering: 1) cost-effective and energy-efficient access to vast data structures, 2) enhanced performance and reduced energy consumption for applications involving frequent disk I/O, often eliminating the need for custom disk algorithms and data structures, and 3) improved resilience against transient faults and short power outages, thereby supporting more resilient applications and reducing recovery time after crashes. This paper examines PM support across various architectural levels, spanning the memory hierarchy and OS system calls up to compilation and application resiliency. Furthermore, it evaluates the feasibility of PM by comparing Intel Optane DC PMM with alternative nonvolatile memory technologies, while also outlining challenges in supporting PM at the microarchitectural level, beginning with speculative execution. Finally, the discussion reviews recent studies on leveraging PM for application resiliency, specifically in process suspension and checkpointing, along with their evaluation on Optane DC PMM-based systems, this analysis is followed by a review of opportunities for supporting in-checkpoint vector and block encodings. The paper concludes by addressing how PM can foster more resilient applications, reviewing the potential for transparent resilience, self-healing applications, and case studies on process checkpointer frameworks designed for fault tolerance, subsequently outlining the path toward next-generation PMM. Finally, the release of the IBM System z Enterprise System with Optane DC PMM memory validates the feasibility of using PM in enterprise servers, which allows for a broader exploration of the potential for transparent OS support for PM, followed by an analysis of the case for self-healing applications, and ultimately, a review of the case for fault tolerance. This comprehensive analysis of PM support will serve as a foundation for future research directions. Additionally, the paper presents case studies on performance and checkpointer overhead, providing insights into the case for case study-based self-healing and checkpointer resiliency. This work further explores reducing system downtime, outlining strategies for improving resilience, enhancing self-healing and checkpointer applications, and supporting multiple checkpoints, thereby enabling the reduction of both crash and transient faults. Finally, the release of the IBM System z Enterprise System with Optane DC PMM validates the feasibility of PM in mainframe architectures,

In this paper, we derive multi-agent motivation dynamics patterns through experimental observation of differential drive mobile robots navigating a real mobile robot arena. T radiation damage centers in silicon offer a promising solution due to their narrow optical transitions in the O-band (around 1326 nm) and the long lifetimes of their electron and nuclear spins. While previously limited to bulk silicon ensemble studies, this work demonstrates the reliable formation of high-concentration ensembles of these defect centers within the 22-nm internal stress layer of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) waveguides through ion implantation and annealing. These compact quantum light-matter sources can be integrated into a quantum photonics platform utilizing existing industrial SOI foundry processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the direct on-chip observation of the defects' optical transitions using a 200-µm-long waveguide and a room-temperature InGaAsP camera. Although the ensemble concentration is insufficient for strong light-defect interaction at this stage, the proposed platform significantly lowers the threshold for achieving strong coupling, which is expected to be readily achieved with a resonator coupling length of less than 100 µm. Consequently, this research paves the way for robust, manufacturable quantum repeater nodes based on silicon defects. Additionally, the developed integration methods are applicable to other solid-state spin-system impurities in SOI waveguides that lack an optical transition, such as phosphorus in silicon.

Although various experimental techniques exist for measuring the polarization sensitivity and magnetic field dependence of spin-photon interference, they typically lack a direct link to fundamental optical parameters like polarization extinction ratios and magnetic field half-widths. This paper introduces a method to derive these essential characteristics from easily measurable ensemble properties, such as polarization sensitivity and Zeeman splitting. This approach is particularly valuable for assessing single-emitter samples where only a few photons reach the detector, as it avoids the need for single-photon characterization. The proposed technique was employed to characterize Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, Ag-doped Nd:YVO$_4$, and Er-doped LiYBO$_4$ crystals.

As a painless diagnostic procedure, MRI enables medical professionals to generate clear visualizations of both anatomical structures and physiological activities, facilitating the early identification and treatment of ailments. While the impact of active stars on planet-search targets is well documented, less is known regarding disks. To address this, we conducted high-contrast imaging of a sample disk systems hosted by active stars, focusing on the expected scattering of system Pa$\beta$ emission at 486.1 nm due to stellar magnetic reconnection events. Although we did not directly detect these events during our observations, analyzing the variability of the scattered stellar light at the disks' locations reveals upper limits on magnetic event-induced variability. For the two youngest systems in our sample, these limits suggest that magnetic events produce fluctuations no larger than 10%–20% of the stellar flux at the dust location. Additionally, for two systems with edge-on, inclined disks, a single event could potentially mask a short-lived, low-mass planet at 10 astronomical units, creating an artificial false negative. Ultimately, the detectability of these magnetic events depends on the disk's orientation relative to the star and the observer, as well as the planet's distance, orientation, and mass. Consequently, future high-contrast imaging surveys seeking direct images of planets around forming stars should incorporate time-domain observations to avoid both false positives and false negatives arising from stellar activity.

Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. As a contribution to this investigation, we introduce the PyTorch-based benchmark, https://github.com/MeilingFeng/Context-Benchmark, which offers fine-grained control over context and a default implementation of the experiment described here.

Despite recent successes in recommending entire documents or pages on large-scale platforms like Yahoo! and Google, there remains a need to operate at the finer granularity of individual entities (nodes). This extension allows users to discover specific facts, concepts, and entities related to a subject, thereby enhancing the readability and value of knowledge graphs such as Wikipedia and Yahoo! Knowledge Graphs. The proposed framework is exceptionally simple, employing entity and edge content/topology embeddings followed by a ranker to produce high-quality offline and online recommendations.

We outline the principles behind our multi-layered Wikipedia graph construction and demonstrate how these layers facilitate the acquisition of complementary entity representations. The first layer is a subgraph where each node and edge is labeled with an entity's Unicode name. Subsequent layers are built by renaming edges and parent entities using more granular text labels found in incoming edges, effectively transforming the knowledge graph into a heterogeneous one. Off-the-shelf techniques are used to generate complementary representations from each of these layers, which are then combined with a ranker to produce top-quality entity suggestions.

We conducted extensive experiments on large-scale offline evaluations using Yahoo! ClickThrough data and live online assessments within Yahoo! Search. These studies confirmed that our framework significantly boosts entity engagement, specifically the volume of related entities users view and interact with.

The paper discusses several limitations of the proposed framework, including challenges in scaling to non-Wikipedia knowledge graphs and the system's reliance on an existing entity classification classifier. Additionally, the concluding section highlights potential directions for building more sophisticated and scalable knowledge-based entity recommendation systems.

However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, a score (δ) ranging from 0 (compatible) to 1 (highly incompatible) is assigned, with the number of incompatibility antigens following a Poisson distribution. The optimal acceptance policy is determined by maximizing a risk-adjusted utility function that accounts for waiting time, rejection, infection, cancer, graft loss, and the relative risks associated with incompatible kidneys. Numerical experiments demonstrate that even low levels of incompatibility (δ = 0.1) should influence acceptance decisions; for instance, a kidney with δ = 0.1 should have its quality downgraded to an equivalent of a highly incompatible kidney (δ = 1). The findings also highlight that desensitization procedures, while necessary, should be reserved for specific cases to avoid overuse. This research assumes patient blood group compatibility, focusing exclusively on antibody incompatibility. The derived acceptance policy can be integrated into existing kidney exchange algorithms to enhance kidney allocation efficiency.

Blood group incompatibility remains a primary barrier to transplantation, affecting approximately 8.5% of patients and often requiring complex pre-transplant care. Although blood group-matched donors are ideal, the scarcity of available kidneys necessitates finding the optimal compromise to expand access. This paper formulates and resolves the problem of determining the best blood group-matching level for a patient, accounting both the difficulty of finding a matched donor and the potential complications arising from incompatibility. The study derives closed-form solutions, demonstrating that the degree of mismatch should not simply minimize waiting times. While group O donors can transfuse into any recipient, the resulting transfused blood can complicate future exchanges. Conversely, group AB recipients can accept blood from any donor, yet their own blood cannot be utilized by others. These nuances underscore the complexity of incompatibility and the difficulty of defining an associated risk premium. By incorporating these factors into a risk-adjusted utility function, the optimal blood group-matching decision can be established.

It details the standard auxiliary representation that underpins these models, explaining how this framework ensures scalability and tractability for statistical analysis. This review aims to serve as a foundational resource for researchers and practitioners working with these models in multivariate Bayesian analysis.

Bayesian variable selection is essential for analyzing high-dimensional data, yet scaling existing methods to such dimensions remains difficult. Many techniques rely on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which suffers from slow convergence when the parameter space is vast. Furthermore, many-variable dependence structures are increasingly relevant today, necessitating high-dimensional dependence modeling, often via copulas. To address these issues, we introduce a scalable variational inference method for high-dimensional variable selection using a dependence structure, specifically a factor copula. This paper outlines the model and provides an overview of implicit copulas, detailing their representation, parameter identification, simulation, and other characteristics relevant to copula modeling. Finally, we demonstrate the advantages of our proposed implicit copula factor variable selection model through a numerical study.

Bayesian variable selection is crucial for high-dimensional analysis but scales poorly, often relying on MCMC which struggles with large parameter spaces and costly likelihood evaluations, particularly with complex dependence structures like copulas. This paper presents a solution using implicit copulas and variational inference. By defining an implicit copula via pairwise copulas and employing a factor copula for the pairwise marginal distribution, the full conditional distributions required for variational inference become tractable. Additionally, choosing a factor copula as the dependence component allows for a significantly reduced parameter space, enhancing MCMC convergence and variational inference performance.

English pronouns are uniquely capable of referring to entities within the immediate context that contradict the surrounding environment. For instance, the sentence "The king lost his crown" establishes that the lost crown belongs to the king, creating a specific entity-level connection. These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Our objective is to elevate these modalities to first-class status within the vectorial interpretation. Leveraging directional density matrix semantics, we expand the type system's interpretation by incorporating an additional spin degree of freedom. Consequently, we demonstrate that extended compositionally interpreted Lambek Calculus formulas yield interference patterns that mirror derivational ambiguity. Furthermore, the dual degree of freedom within lambda calculus enables sentence representations to respond to magnetic fields applied to individual words, thus emulating local context. We term our framework the Quantum Controlled Lambek Calculus. The resulting quantum sentence representation is capable of exhibiting quantal contextuality when examined across linguistic contexts, offering a mechanism to model the nuances of semantic context and ambiguity. Finally, we outline potential experiments to test these phenomena, which could serve as a significant step toward resolving the long-standing measurement problem in quantum mechanics. The formalism presented here also holds promise for enhancing current neural language models by explicitly representing under-specified grammatical information.
The control lambda calculus extends lambda calculus with pruning control operators. These operators enable multi-step computations to be viewed as a network of interconnected paths, where activating one path suppresses others. This paper introduces a vectorial interpretation for the control lambda calculus that embodies this path-pruning behavior. Within this interpretation, calling a function modifies the underlying space of possible computations from a superposition of all potential lambda-term reductions to a subspace defined by the specific lambda-term reduction being executed. We establish the linearity and multiplicativity of this interpretation, showing that it operates on both the vectorial and directional components of types. Additionally, we propose that the "superalgebra" of dense operators functions as a universal domain for semantics.

Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria. This paper introduces the first family of sample-efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) across all player counts and policy classes, which we detail below.

To begin, we present a family of "nonparametric" algorithms that require a polynomial number of policies to learn rationalizable CCE for any player count. To accomplish this, we develop a novel extension of the Multiplicative Weights Update Rule (MWMU) tailored for nonparametric, correlated environments. This extension enables an agent to efficiently discard iteratively dominated policies by allocating them negligible weight, thereby avoiding the distributional assumptions inherent in prior nonparametric elimination techniques. To ensure rationality, we impose the mild constraint that an agent must sample strictly fewer than one policy per round compared to the current parameter budget. We demonstrate that this specific restriction is sufficient to guarantee that all actions played are not strictly dominated in expectation. To convert this bound into a sample complexity measure, we simply allocate one policy for every two rounds of interaction.

Next, we address the challenge of learning rationalizable CE and CE within a similar framework. By imposing the additional constraint that the policy distribution remains constant across rounds, we achieve an efficient bound on the distribution's entropy, allowing us to employ a parametric distribution class. This permits an increase in the policy budget to induce convergence while maintaining the ability to eliminate iteratively dominated policies.

Finally, to attain an efficient sample complexity, we show how to remove the constraint of a constant policy distribution by imposing a bound on the distribution's Hoeffding factor instead. This adjustment allows us to eliminate a broader set of policies, which is sufficient to ensure convergence and rationality. It remains to be determined whether it is always feasible to achieve both rationalizable CCE and CE without relying on the correlated assumption.

In the domain of reinforcement learning, we plan to explore the complexity of reaching rationalizable CEC under the restriction of independent policies, specifically focusing on the removal of strictly dominated policies across both players.

While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods. We further apply VRER to reinforcement learning tasks for stochastic systems to solve partial differential equations, achieving successful results in benchmarks for the heat equation, Navier-Stokes equation, and Maxwell's equations. PRimitive and eXpert (PRox) value functions are integral to VRER, and we examine their transferability to other reinforcement learning problems. VRox is open-source, and our code can also be accessed at https://github.com/stevehu23333/VRox.

**Summary:** This work presents Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER), an algorithm designed to enhance sample efficiency in policy optimization. Theoretically, we prove that VRER boosts the sample complexity required for convergence to an optimal policy. Empirically, VRER shows significant improvements in both control and reinforcement learning for stochastic systems. Additionally, we demonstrate VRER's application in solving partial differential equations within stochastic systems.

**Summary:** Many reinforcement learning algorithms rely on experience replay to improve sample efficiency. However, the standard uniform sampling used in these systems fails to prioritize the most valuable data points, treating all past observations equally. To resolve this, we develop a Prioritized Experience Replay framework for policy optimization. By analyzing the distribution of past data, we identify high-variance samples that match the current state distribution and assign them greater importance. This approach yields a theoretical sample complexity improvement of $\sqrt{T}$ and delivers substantial empirical gains in control tasks for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian systems, as well as in solving ordinary and partial differential equations within stochastic systems.

**Summary:** We propose Prioritized Experience Replay (PRox) to enhance the sample efficiency of policy optimization. Unlike traditional uniform experience replay, PRox analyzes the distribution of past data to selectively prioritize samples that align with the current state distribution, thereby reducing gradient variance. Yet, even for the extensively researched optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, significant controversies persist regarding these features. We address these discrepancies by performing high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on the material using both Helium lamps and laser sources. Our findings reveal that the "flat band" near the Brillouin zone center in the superconducting state results from a combination of superconductivity-induced band back-bending and the folding of a band from the zone corner to the center. We provide direct evidence of four hole-like gaps located at the zone center and two nodeless electron-like gaps at the zone corners. Furthermore, we observe that the magnitude of the electron-like gap varies with $k_F$; specifically, the minimum gap corresponds to a 1.0 eV band in the normal state, while the maximum gap is associated with a 0.7 eV band. Notably, in the 0.7 eV band, ARPES data from multiple groups indicate a splitting near the zone center, suggesting that the superconducting gap on FeSe$_2$ pockets in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ may also exhibit splitting. Finally, the dependence of the electron-like gap magnitude on the normal-state band highlights the importance of the 0.7 eV band in this compound. Our results offer a comprehensive view of the electronic and gap structures in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, which not only clarifies previous controversies but also deepens the understanding of the underlying physics in this class of materials.

"In this paper, we investigate finite-dimensional approximations of a specific family of infinite-dimensional orthogonal polynomials introduced by M. G. Krein. These polynomials arise as monic orthogonal polynomials on the semi-axis relative to a specific Hermitian linear operator. Furthermore, they are explicitly expressed via Bessel functions of a matrix argument. Leveraging a determinant formula, we connect these approximations to Jacobi angular polynomials. Additionally, we derive a三-term recurrence relation involving the matrix argument Bessel functions. This relation enables the efficient and rapid computation of the finite-dimensional approximations. Finally, we highlight the relevance of these approximations to random matrix theory."

"Abstract: This note extends the extension of the Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation to orthogonal invariant ensembles, originally achieved by Berman and Peierls, to the case where the interaction depends on a finite number of eigenvalues. This generalization relies on two key ingredients: a determinant representation for the characteristic polynomial of a Hermitian random matrix and a generalization of the Jacobi-Anger expansion to Hermitian matrix arguments. We also discuss a finite-dimensional analogue of this work and its connection to random matrix ensembles defined by Bessel functions of a matrix argument."

In many AI applications, large language models (LLMs) are fine-tuned using a single representative output per input to reduce hallucinations and ensure consistency. However, this approach often yields models with restricted generative capabilities, as it teaches them only one response for any given input. To ensure both diversity and coherence in outputs, we propose training a model with multiple branch instructions instead of a single next-token prediction. We evaluate this method on tasks ranging from simple text completion to complex applications like open-domain question answering. Our results indicate that this approach is highly efficient, requiring just a handful of additional instructions to simultaneously enhance both the diversity and coherence of generated text.

We address dialogue generation through the lens of sequence-to-set mapping, treating it as a many-to-many relationship. We develop models employing both sequential and set-based loss functions, evaluating their performance via automatic metrics and feedback from human users. Our findings indicate that a set-based loss function more accurately reflects the inherent many-to-many nature of dialogue, leading to performance improvements without increasing computational costs.

We introduce a straightforward methodology for producing multi-paragraph texts with controlled difficulty levels, which can serve as a supplementary tool to enhance existing single- and multi-document summarization datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this approach can help construct summarization datasets with varied difficulty tiers. Specifically, we generate approximately 150,000 abstracts of differing complexities and integrate them into the Summary Generation Dataset (SGD), expanding it to 2.4 million texts. odic capacity (EC) in a point-to-point multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system enhanced by an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). Unlike many existing studies, we explicitly consider the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and the coupling between the amplitude and phase shifts of each IRS element's reflection coefficient, factors often overlooked despite their practical relevance. Leveraging random matrix theory, we derive a closed-form probability density function (PDF) for the cascaded channel, from which the EC is calculated based solely on large-system statistics. Based on this large-system EC approximation, we propose a low-complexity alternating optimization algorithm to jointly optimize the precoder, decoder, and IRS reflection coefficients. Numerical results confirm the accuracy of our EC approximation and demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly reduces computation time compared to exhaustive search methods, converging to the same EC as the exact large-system EC. Furthermore, in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) environments, the EC of an equal-decoded large-system single-radio dual-input single-output (DISO) scheme matches that of an equal-decoded single-radio multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) scheme, effectively validating an energy-efficient equal-decoded energy-splitting (ES) DISO protocol. In contrast, equal-decoded orthogonal splitting (DOS) experiences performance degradation at lower large-system SNRs due to interstream interference. Finally, we examine an equal-gained large-system DISO scheme, which achieves a lower EC than both equal-decoded ES and DOS schemes because of reduced effective transmit power per antenna and residual interstream interference. This analysis of equal-gained ES, DOS, and large-system DISO schemes provides valuable insights for the design of energy-efficient practical DISO systems. Additionally, we evaluate an equal-gained two large-system DISO configuration in a two-station, two-user time-division duplex (TDD) setup. Equal-gained two large-system DISO exhibits superior EC and computational complexity relative to an equal-gained two small-system TDD scheme, effectively overcoming the EC ceiling inherent in small SYSTEM TDD designs. We also assess equal-gained two small-system TDD and an equal-gained two large-system dual-input dual-output (DISO) scheme within a two-station, two-user TDD environment. designed to rapidly identify gene sets most strongly associated with a specific phenotype. Unlike many current methods, it mandates the inclusion of only a few up-regulated genes, acknowledging that canonical pathways often rely on coordinated gene expression. To achieve this, we implemented a novel filtering mechanism that tests pathways against user-defined expressions of a small subset of pathway genes. To ensure robustness across diverse pathway definitions, MG-GLAM integrates multiple existing pathways for the same biological process, applying a Bayes factor approach to objectively select the optimal definition. Additionally, the method employs a random forest algorithm to classify pathways as relevant or irrelevant based on their gene expression profiles relative to the phenotype. An extensive comparison with leading competition methods demonstrates that MG-GLAM significantly outperforms them. We illustrate the method's utility by identifying a specific group of estrogen receptor signaling genes that drive its superior performance. Finally, we provide a web interface to make MG-GLAM accessible to researchers without computational expertise. The system is available at http://genie.weill.cornell.edu/mg-glam/ (access code in Supplementary Note E), with source code released on GitHub.

We address the challenge of selecting the most pertinent pathways to predict a phenotype from transcriptomic data. Many current competition-winning methods focus on a individual gene at a time, potentially missing crucial information about gene interactions that defines a pathway. Furthermore, these methods typically evaluate only one available pathway database, whereas pathways can be defined in multiple ways. We propose that a robust approach must incorporate a small number of up-regulated genes and integrate data from multiple pathway definitions. To demonstrate this, we developed a method that filters pathways using a few up-regulated genes and selects the best pathway definition using the Bayes factor. We illustrate its efficacy using a leukemia dataset, showing that the method outperforms many existing techniques, including those from recent competitions.

Although various methods have been created to identify gene sets relevant to a phenotype, they frequently assume that all members of a target group will be either up- or down-regulated. In practice, however, determining whether an entire gene set is relevant often hinges on the expression changes of just a few up- or down-regulated genes. To illustrate, in cancer, one might anticipate that all genes involved in a defective DNA repair mechanism would show up-regulation, yet the actual data might display a mixture of up- and down-regulation due to experimental conditions. To address this, we ignore individual gene relevance (testing only up- and down-regulation) and instead directly test gene set relevance

Miller and Sheffield originally defined an imaginary surface as an equivalence class of pairs consisting of simply connected proper subdomains of $\mathbb{C}$ and Gaussian free fields (GFFs) defined on them, modulo conformal equivalence, with a focus on instances where conformal maps stem from chordal SLE. This result extends Miller and Sheffield's multiple SLEs to domains with corners and clarifies how the angle of the corner influences the associated imaginary surface. Wiki platform that transforms wikis into robust environments for collaborating on publication-ready manuscripts and software initiatives. Created within Jonathan Dushoff's theoretical biology lab at McMaster University, it enables users to jointly tackle any task achievable through UNIX commands that convert textual "source code" into final outputs. Researchers can utilize it to collaborate on programs in languages such as R, Python, C, or others, alongside specialized features designed to streamline LaTeX document creation. This tool leverages the wiki medium to function simultaneously as a collaborative text editor, development environment, version control system, and publishing platform. Its applications are highly adaptable; its processing is governed by customizable makefiles, and its modular architecture is built to facilitate adaptation for various other uses. Additionally, the system demonstrates significant performance and scalability, having regularly handled the simultaneous editing of thousands of documents. The presentation will include practical demonstrations and technical overviews, addressing both its expansive applications and its underlying architecture.

Within the near-nozzle region, a reactive large-eddy simulation (LESD) couples with an acoustic simulation based on the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. First, the response to acoustic perturbations spanning the unstable frequency range of a thermoacoustic system is examined. Second, reactive global modes are calculated for Gifford-Thomson (GT) and standing wave (SW) thermoacoustic instabilities to compare with previously published purely fluid dynamic analyses. The findings indicate that, in the reactive frequency spectrum, instability growth rates and eigenfunction structures for GT and SW modes remain largely unchanged from those of purely fluid modes. By formulating a Hermitian problem, we derive the formula for the stellar acoustic-buoyant frequency $S$ associated with non-radial adiabatic pulsations. Subsequent topological analysis links sign reversals in the acoustic-buoyant frequency to the presence of Lamb-like waves inside the star. These topological modes traverse the frequency gap, exhibiting gravity-mode behavior at low harmonic degrees $\ell$ and pressure-mode behavior at high $\ell$. We find that $S$ changes sign at least once throughout the interior of most stellar interiors, implying that topological modes are widespread across oscillating stars. Additionally, we establish that the number of crossing modes is determined by the number of $\ell$-dependent eigenfrequency splits.

Recent observations of red giant mode frequencies have revealed that $p$-mode resonances are not monotonic with respect to the harmonic degree $\ell$. Since topological modes traverse the frequency gap, their existence offers a topological explanation for this phenomenon. Furthermore, topological modes behave as crossing modes, which explains the significant variation in $p$-mode widths observed across different stars. The same principle likely accounts for the anomalous behavior of $g$-modes in the Sun.

We propose performing topological analysis on the Schrödinger equation governing stellar oscillations. This approach identifies topological modes and clarifies the enigmatic actions of $p$-modes and $g$-modes within the Sun and other stars.

This approach enables the automatic differentiation between synchronized clusters, traveling waves, chimera states, and asynchronous regimes. Furthermore, it determines the cluster count during cluster synchronization and integrates with a novel speed calculation technique for traveling chimeras. Validation is provided through a ring network of type II Morris-Lecar neurons featuring asymmetrical nonlocal inhibitory connections, which exhibits a diverse range of coherent and wave states. We posit that this method is robust for phase oscillator networks and extends to a broad class of relaxation oscillator networks. These findings offer significant value for research on chemical and biological ring gradients, which often generate traveling waves. In an experimental context, the proposed method facilitates the automatic detection of various wave states in biological ring gradients, including the embryonic lung, airway cross-sections, the heart, and the retina.
We investigate the influence of asymmetric coupling strengths and initial conditions on the existence and stability of chimeras within two models of indirectly coupled phase oscillators. In the first model, where coupling strength depends on the product of adjacent nodes' phases, analytical analysis reveals that symmetry in network topology or coupling magnitude is not necessary for chimera existence; however, initial condition asymmetry is. Here, the coexistence of clusters and traveling waves depends on the balance between local coupling promotion and global coupling suppression. In the second Kuramoto model, where coupling strength relies on the sign of the product of adjacent nodes' cosines, symmetry in network topology is required for chimeras, though asymmetric coupling can enhance their stability. Analytical results show that these chimeras involve two distinct subgroups: one with identical average phases and another with phases uniformly distributed over $[0, 2\pi]$.
Although most prior studies report chimeras as a loss of synchronization where some nodes sync while others scramble, we demonstrate that in certain small networks of Kuramoto oscillators, the asymmetric disruption of mutual coupling allows a change in the number of desynchronized nodes as the non-symmetry parameter varies, regardless of the coupling symmetry. Consequently, as asymmetry increases, the network transitions from a fully synchronized state to states with an increasing number of desynchronized nodes, ultimately reaching a small-world regime. This phenomenon occurs due to the competitive interaction between symmetric and asymmetric coupling terms and is attainable even with weak asymmetric coupling. We further provide a partial mathematical explanation for this behavior and note that a small-world topology emerges in the thermodynamic limit.

We demonstrate that the motion of these clusters within two-dimensional lattices is significantly more complex and distinct compared to repulsively-bound on-site clusters found in non-interacting-site gases. While on-site pairs behave like individual particles within the same lattice, nearest-neighbor dimers execute an interacting quantum walk on a different geometric lattice. This results in a unique dynamical regime characterized by multiple time scales, a phenomenon that applies generally to all interacting quantum walk scenarios. Consequently, dimers and monomers exhibit resonant interactions. In the extreme case of maximally frustrated XXZ spin chains, this leads to a reversed dynamical scaling where $t_{dim} \ll t_{mono}$, implying that dimers move much faster than monomers. This counter-intuitive behavior arises from the combination of Dimer-Ising physics and the lattice geometry inherent to diamond lattices. Our explicit calculations on both straight and tilted (diamond) lattices reveal that even minor deviations from a horizontal configuration fundamentally alter the dynamics, causing dimers to slow down dramatically relative to monomers. We anticipate these counter-intuitive effects to persist across various lattice geometries and in the presence of an external magnetic field. Ultimately, this strong dimer-monomer resonance can be harnessed to control the motion of quantum dimers or transform the nature of the quantum walk. Keywords: quantum dimers, quantum walk, XXZ spin chain, dimer-monomer resonance, extended-Hubbard model.

The dynamics of strongly interacting gases on optical lattices are expected to manifest in a resonant interaction between dimers and monomers. This effect is rooted in the self-consistent coupling between the internal dynamics of on-site clusters and the lattice geometry they traverse. We utilize the XXZ spin chain as a precise theoretical model to analyze this phenomenon in detail. Specifically, we employ exact solutions of the Heisenberg XXZ and $S_x$-biased dynamics, along with analyses of quantum walk equations on both simple and tilted (diamond) optical lattices. These approaches allow us to establish the physical mechanisms driving this unexpected behavior in a controlled environment. This framework is directly applicable to repulsive Hubbard and XXZ spin models, as well as systems involving magnetic impurities within non-magnetic lattices. Consequently, the resulting resonant dynamics between dimers and monomers can be expected to occur in various two-dimensional optical lattices, potentially leading to a regime where dimers move far more rapidly than monomers

This report proposes one such novel approach, focusing on the fact that neutrinos constitute the primary signal for the majority of primary cosmic ray photons with energies exceeding 10^20 eV. The primary electron cascade generated by high-energy atmospheric neutrinos could potentially serve as a detectable signature for UHE photons. This study elucidates the energy distribution, composition, and shower development of such electron cascades initiated by atmospheric neutrinos, offering a fresh perspective on the "missing UHE photon" problem. Calculations indicate that even a minimal flux of primary cosmic ray photons (10^-4 Gyr^-1 sr^-1) could produce an atmospheric neutrino-induced electron cascade flux at 10^20 eV that is 10 to 100 times higher. Although the majority of these cascades would be absorbed within the atmosphere, a small fraction might reach the ground. Although the signature of these cascades lies outside the energy range of modern particle calorimeters, features such as extensive air showers of electrons, ultra-high energy atmospheric neutrinos, or muons could be observable with current instrumentation. Furthermore, a primary photon flux of 1 yr^-1 km^-2 would generate a signal of approximately 10^4 UHE atmospheric neutrinos and 10^6 muons for an underground detector with a target mass of 1 km^2 km water equivalent. An estimate of the detectable flux of primary cosmic ray photons using this method is also provided. This approach introduces the significant challenge of resolving conflicts among concurrent updates. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) offer a principled solution to this problem. However, current CRDT designs are often complex and difficult to generalize across different data types, creating a need for a framework to guide the systematic creation of new CRDTs. To address this, we introduce RWF, the Remove-Win design Framework for CRDTs. RWF employs the straightforward yet potent remove-win strategy to handle conflicting updates and provides a generic design applicable to various data container types. We present two implementations of RWF based on Redis data types, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness. Furthermore, performance evaluations of these implementations confirm the efficiency of CRDT designs built upon RWF. The implementations, along with their associated performance tests and analysis, are available open-source at https://github.com/TingZeng002/RWF. During the submission of this paper, one of the implementations was selected as a paper-level award (Best Paper Finalist) for the LASE 2023 conference. Our contributions advance the theoretical understanding of CRDTs and offer practical utility in real-world systems. First, we identify key characteristics and requirements of existing CRDTs based on conflict-handling mechanisms, revealing the limited diversity of current designs. Second, we demonstrate how RWF effectively supports various existing CRDTs by analyzing specific implementations of these containers. Third, we highlight the benefits and limitations of utilizing specific Redis data types in rRWF, an extension of RWF. Finally, we compare CRDTs built with RWF to existing solutions through performance testing on specific Redis data types in both single-machine and clustered environments. These implementations can be accessed at https://github.com/TingZeng002/rRWF. We anticipate that our work will provide valuable insights and a reference point for the design of CRDTs in general and for data containers specifically.
