This work introduces an effective-theory framework based on soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) to integrate massive (bottom) quark effects into resummed differential distributions. This approach accounts for both primary contributions from heavy-quark initiated hard scattering and secondary effects stemming from gluons splitting into heavy-quark pairs. Specifically, we examine the Drell-Yan process, focusing on the vector-boson transverse momentum ($q_T$) and beam thrust ($\mathcal T$) as representative exclusive observables. The theoretical formulation relies on the hierarchy among the hard scale, the quark mass, and the $q_T$ (or $\mathcal T$) scale, spanning from the decoupling limit ($q_T \ll m$) to the massless limit ($m \ll q_T$). The phenomenologically critical intermediate regime ($m \sim q_T$) necessitates the use of quark-mass dependent beam and soft functions. We compute all necessary components for describing both primary and secondary mass effects at NNLL$'$ resummation order—combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions—for both $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all relevant scales. For the $q_T$ distribution, we note that rapidity divergences differ from the massless scenario and discuss the characteristics of the associated beam functions. Regarding the $\mathcal T$ distribution, we derive the requisite NNLO beam and soft functions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of mass effects on the $q_T$ distribution, noting that recent measurements by ATLAS constrain the sum of strong and electroweak contributions. Our findings indicate that secondary mass effects become comparable to electroweak effects when $q_T$ falls below 3% of the Drell-Yan invariant mass, an observation that remains significant even at very low $q_T$. Finally, we extend our discussion to the $q_T$ distribution in Higgs boson production. Additional remarks address issues concerning perturbative convergence and the necessary matching to fixed-order calculations. Additionally, we examine the massless limit of both formulations and confirm that they yield identical results. This formalism is designed for integration with recent massless building blocks, enabling the systematic exploration of higher-order theoretical precision. Additional research topics regarding this formalism include incorporating effects from heavy-quark decays and refining the description of the $q_T$ distribution in Higgs production through contributions from flavor

While the velocity gauge, which relies on linear coupling to the vector potential, is the conventional approach for describing optical properties, it relies on quasi-periodic boundary conditions that complicate its application to finite systems. Furthermore, the equivalence between this gauge and the dipole approximation remains uncertain for materials with large unit cells or those possessing broken translational symmetry, such as spiraling metallic TB models. We calculate the optical conductivity of these models using both the velocity gauge and dipole approximation within the TB framework, comparing the results against exact supercell calculations based on plane-wave methods. Additionally, we explore formulating the velocity gauge for finite systems by extending the Bloch wavefunction to include additional terms that explicitly depend on system size. Our findings indicate that the dipole approximation and the extended Bloch wavefunction approach yield results for finite systems that converge to exact supercell outcomes in the infinite-system limit, with only minor corrections required for finite systems having a volume comparable to the unit cell. In contrast, the standard velocity gauge application to periodic systems shows significant deviations when applied to finite systems, especially those with volumes similar to the unit cell. We also form a complete theoretical argument supporting these observations, which is validated against the numerical experiments, offering insights into forming tight-binding models for few-layer van der Waals heterostructures with moiré superlattices. Finally, we note that the formalism developed here can be readily extended to incorporate spin-orbit coupling and non-Abelian vector potentials, which are essential for accurately modeling systems involving spin-triplet states, such as those encountered in quantum Hall physics. This research is strictly computational in nature, relying entirely on numerical experiments for its conclusions.

Formalizing natural language instructions into executable code represents a critical capability for advanced language models. We introduce a multi-turn instruction tuning technique utilizing a synthetic dataset composed of code pairs derived from existing function-level instructions. These instructions are obtained by extracting and modifying signatures and implementations from open-source repositories, utilizing the original signatures as query prompts to generate full-function implementations via a pre-trained code completion model. Unlike existing techniques that rely on large-scale instruction tuning, our experiments demonstrate that training for just a few iterations on this dataset is sufficient to significantly enhance the instruction following and coding performance of models trained to approximately the scale of Instruction Tuning (IT) 50B. Specifically, when the network comprises a single type of tensor that also acts as an erasure correction code, we demonstrate that it is impossible to simultaneously achieve local contractibility and sustain power-law correlations. Driven by this no-go theorem and the necessity of local contractibility for efficient variational ansätze, we offer guidelines for designing networks with multiple tensor types that can support power-law correlations. Furthermore, we present an explicit construction of such a network, which approximates the holographic HaPPY pentagon code in the limit where variational parameters approach zero. We also explore connections to recent findings regarding local unit cell structures in continuously contractible quantum error correction codes with topological and power-law stabilizers. Additional results include proving the inability of network types locally equivalent to the Peierls-Aronovskyt network to correct erasures, and showing that networks based on T-splits cannot sustain sublinear correlation functions. Finally, we outline potential extensions involving networks with directed edges and those composed of approximate sum codes. This work is intended to serve as a reference for constructing holographic tensor networks that function as both variational ansätze and error correction codes.

We analyze the universality class of a random fixed point governing two-dimensional two-component random walks with long-range correlations. These walks constitute the primary object of study within the random sequential adhesion model. Based on field-theoretic arguments, numerical simulations, and analytical exact results, we find that these random walks exhibit a branching process dynamic. We also establish a link to the long-time behavior of the random long-range contact process. Our results indicate that the critical interaction range is given by $r_{c} = 2.69(5)$. We provide descriptions of two related models: randomly long-range random walks and conditioned long-range random walks. Our investigation of the randomly long-range random walk reveals it shares the same universality class as its unrandomized version. However, the conditioned long-range random walk exhibits distinct critical exponents, though it remains within the same universality class as the random fixed point. These observations offer a comprehensive understanding of the modeling of long-range correlations.

Results indicated that steady-state reaction quantum yields (observed at 10 ps and later) differ markedly from transient values, implying a weak link between transient behavior and steady-state dynamics in these systems. Notably, while transient dynamics remained largely insensitive to minor parameter variations, the steady-state quantum yield exhibited high sensitivity to such minute changes. Rooted in standard non-equilibrium statistical physics, this phenomenon is connected to a singularity arising from the divergence of the density of states near an exact level crossing. The study questions the universal applicability of design principles derived from transient dynamics to optimize reaction quantum yields. Furthermore, the paper argues that the Markovian master equation model, often employed to elucidate shape recovery in bovine rhodopsin, lacks unique solution stability and is poorly suited for exploring parameter sensitivity in complex systems like vision proteins. The persistent global challenge of accurately predicting the three-dimensional structures of non-redundant amino acid sequences remains a central focus of contemporary bioinformatics. While deep learning methods have recently surpassed hand-crafted approaches in this prediction task, their learned representations have thus far failed to exhibit meaningful behavior when examined outside the context of accurate three-dimensional folding. This work introduces a straightforward learning framework for contact probability maps that successfully incorporates insights gained from the physics of polymer science. Although trained exclusively on alpha-helical and beta-strand rich proteins, the model generalizes effectively to contact probability predictions across all secondary structure types. Most significantly, we demonstrate that the implicit representation of three-dimensional structures encoded within this model contains sufficient information to train a contact predictor for the Q3 structure prediction task, thereby outperforming any model pretrained solely on Q3 data. These findings suggest that contemporary deep learning techniques for three-dimensional structure prediction are unlikely to achieve a substantial breakthrough without integrating prior knowledge about polymer physics.

Although most prior research has focused on the information content of DNA sequences, it is well established that a protein's three-dimensional structure is the primary determinant of its function. While a protein's sequence dictates its final three-dimensional conformation, the direct relationship between sequence and function remains obscure. This study investigates whether proteins sharing identical three-dimensional structures, as defined by scaffold metrics, also share similar functional characteristics. Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have proven effective in process mining, surpassing traditional methods in predictive performance. Building on this foundation, we evaluate four Graph Neural Network (GNN) variants alongside a dropout-enhanced fully connected Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) to forecast the next activity's nature and timestamp. Unlike prior studies, we assess model efficacy across various process stages, segmented by quartiles of event counts and normalized case durations. This approach reveals that model behavior varies significantly throughout a business process. Notably, our experiments indicate that the straightforward MLP frequently outperforms more complex deep-learning architectures in both prediction tasks. Consequently, we emphasize the need for caution when deploying automated prediction techniques at different process phases and advocate for researchers to validate their findings against robust baselines such as simple MLPs. Finally, we present techniques for visually displaying activity predictions and their uncertainty, highlighting how historical probability distributions can illuminate potential future activities. The source code for all experiments and predictions is available开源.

We introduce a novel technique for snapping traces to signed distance functions (SDFs) to identify repetitive patterns and anomalies within process data. Building on this, we develop an algorithm to forecast the next activity based on the current process state. Our methods were evaluated and compared against ten existing state-of-the-art approaches on three real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our snapping technique accurately captures process behavior and achieves predictive performance comparable to the leading methods in both activity classification and estimation. Furthermore, the generated snapshots enable the visualization of process behavior across multiple granularities. Finally, our forecasts successfully highlight deviations and inconsistencies in process execution.

Although Markov Models (MM) and their extensions are widely acknowledged as marking a shift towards more accurate marking techniques, they remain underutilized due to a perceived complexity in calculation that marks them as difficult to implement. We demonstrate that constructing a MM is, in fact, a straightforward task. Additionally, we show that these models are highly effective for marking purposes and perform at least as well as, if not better than, complex state-of-the-art Markov Random Field (MRF) models. Our experimental findings confirm that Markov Models can accurately predict approximately 11% of activities, while also capturing marking information for the remaining 89% of activities to a satisfactory degree. We further provide techniques for visualizing process marking predictions and discuss how processes can be colored based on both predicted marking data and probability distributions. As with all experiments conducted, our source code is available at: https://github.com/andreas24

Social media offers a valuable avenue for understanding public sentiment, which can inform both disaster management strategies and public relations efforts. This study examines Twitter data regarding the October 2020 Izmir Earthquake to determine if such analysis can facilitate timely social inferences. To achieve this, the research employs data mining and natural language processing (NLP) techniques, specifically utilizing the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) algorithm for topic modeling and the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment analysis. The findings reveal that users expressed solidarity and a desire to contribute to relief efforts, while also seeking recognition from relevant authorities. The study concludes that the proposed methodologies are effective, with a discussion on directions for future research.

These data are vital for evaluating biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres and calculating surface UV radiation doses for habitable zone planets orbiting low-mass stars. However, a significant constraint in these evaluations is the scarcity of near-ultraviolet spectral observations of stellar flares. This scarcity stems from a general lack of flare data in the ultraviolet range in existing optical datasets, as well as the historically limited availability of high-resolution ultraviolet space telescopes. To address this, we employed the Spectroscopic and Photometric Monitoring of Stars (SAPMOS) pipeline to integrate uvit observations from the TESS mission with sapmos optical data from TESS, SAPMOS on the 1.5-metre telescope at La Silla, and ground-based data from SAPMOS/CoCoRaHS on the 1.0-metre telescope at Sacramento Mount Hamilton. Our analysis successfully recovered optical flare metrics from the optical data and reconstructed the entire flare spectrum in the ultraviolet range for ten flaring white stars. These results demonstrate that combining SAPMOS optical data with uvit data can recover approximately 10% of uvit's aperture dose during a flare event. Consequently, we can extrapolate optical flare metrics to estimate the ultraviolet aperture dose for approximately 40% of the observed energy for specific spectral lines using the SAPMOS/CoCoRaHS spectrum. This extrapolation allows for the recovery of approximately 2.5 times more ultraviolet energy from optical data than previously estimated using optical alone. Our findings suggest that for every uvit observation of a white-dwarf flare conducted between 2016 and 2025, there are roughly four observations of similar precision feasible using optical data. Similarly, for each optical observation of a white-dwarf flare, about ten observations of comparable accuracy can be made using ultraviolet data. These ratios are especially relevant for estimating surface radiation doses for rocky planets in the habitable zones of active, low-mass low-luminosity main-sequence stars. These ratios serve as a foundational step toward reconstructing entire stellar flare spectra from optical data for low-mass main-sequence stars using the TESS mission. Our findings also underscore the need for continued optical monitoring of white-light flares to enable the reconstruction of entire stellar flare spectra, including those in the near-ultraviolet range, from optical data.

We derive rigorous, exact analytical expressions governing wave propagation, bi-directional reflectionless transmission, and coherent perfect absorption and lasing (CPAL) in such finite periodic optical systems. By leveraging a generalized parametric space—constructed from PT-symmetric transfer matrices, the Lorentz reciprocity theorem, and non-imaginary Bloch phases—we demonstrate that when a unit cell operates in the PT-broken phase or at an exceptional point, propagating modes are guaranteed regardless of the unit cell count or transmission phase. Conversely, in the exact PT-symmetric phase, the existence of propagating waves relies on the unit cell's transmission phase. Notably, we identify that bi-directional reflectionless behavior with unity transmittance can be achieved even outside the exceptional point, provided the number of unit cells and specific PT phases are carefully selected. Furthermore, we propose two distinct methods for realizing CPAL: utilizing an odd number of unit cells at the CPAL point, or manipulating a specific broken phase with a precise cell number while nullifying the transmission phase. We conclude that this work provides a solid theoretical foundation for exploring extraordinary wave phenomena in PT-symmetric photonics and suggests new pathways for light manipulation. This research also underscores the significant potential of PT-symmetric periodic waveguide structures for future optical wave manipulation applications.

We propose investigating the propagation of electromagnetic waves through a one-dimensional periodic array of identical meta-atoms labeled by index $n$, where the field distribution of an $n$-th atom is described by a vector $\mathbf{f}_n$. Assuming weak coupling between adjacent atoms, we derive an effective non-Hermitian tight-binding model characterized by hopping amplitudes $t_{n,n\pm 1}$ between neighboring sites. We examine a specific configuration where the left and right hopping amplitudes satisfy $t_{L,n} = t^*_{R,n+1}$, indicating PT-symmetry. This symmetry allows us to derive an exact dispersion relation for a periodic array. Our analysis reveals that regardless of the number of meta-atomic units, the spectrum consistently includes a sub-band of propagating modes with zero group velocity. Additionally, we identify conditions under which the dispersion relation becomes linear, rendering the wave packet's group velocity independent of frequency. This result opens the possibility of observing extraordinary transmission through a screen perforated with such a periodic array.

dynamics of spatially confined vapor-liquid clouds using Gibbs' variational principle as a framework. Specifically, we construct approximate equilibrium states by minimizing the grand potential and analyze transitions between these states under varying grand potentials. Additionally, we examine dynamical evolution from out-of-equilibrium initial conditions derived experimentally, simulating processes within a magnetic trap. Our findings demonstrate that equation of state alone is insufficient to describe magnetic cloud dynamics. We further identify the conditions under which the initial expansion can be considered diffusive versus hydrodynamic, offering a qualitative explanation for the previously observed "freezing" phenomenon. Finally, we show how a dimensionless parameter, previously reported in literature, serves to distinguish between hydrodynamic and diffusive regimes during the expansion of one-component fluids in magnetic traps. This parameter is found to correspond to the Reynolds number. Our results indicate that when the Reynolds number is much greater than one, hydrodynamic behavior dominates, allowing for the application of fluid dynamics principles such as the creation of vortices in rotating frames. These findings are particularly relevant for the interpretation of quantum simulation experiments conducted with one-component Bose-Einstein condensates in magnetic traps.

Equations of state, including the Thomas-Fermi approximation, are insufficient for describing the dynamics of magnetic vapor-liquid clouds. We demonstrate this by comparing predictions from the full many-body Gibbs formalism against those of the Thomas-Fermi approach. While both methods yield comparable results for equilibrated systems, significant discrepancies arise when the systems are out of equilibrium. This discrepancy stems from the inability of the Thomas-Fermi approximation to account for vapor-liquid phase coexistence. While the Gibbs formalism predicts a diffusive expansion, the Thomas-Fermi approximation leads to a hydrodynamic description. We note that a different one-body approximation supports a hydrodynamic view even without phase coexistence; however, this is invalid when interatomic interactions are represented by a Lennard-Jones potential, as higher-order terms in the expansion of the free energy functional cause the hydrodynamic regime to collapse at short length scales. We conclude that the Thomas-Fermi approximation, the equation of state, and the specific form of the interatomic potential are all critical factors in determining whether the dynamics are hydrodynamic or diffusive. Under certain conditions, the Reynolds number can be employed to differentiate between these regimes.

Nevertheless, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to deceive predictions through stealthy semantic transformations like rotation and tapering. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that delivers tight and scalable robustness guarantees for point cloud models against such attacks. We begin by classifying common 3D transformations into three groups: additive (e.g., shearing), composable (e.g., rotation), and indirectly composable (e.g., tapering), offering generic robustness certification strategies for each category. Subsequently, we define specialized certification protocols for various specific semantic transformations and their combinations. Extensive experiments on multiple common 3D transformations demonstrate that TPC significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our framework increases certified accuracy against twisting transformations along the z-axis (within 20°) from 20.3% to 83.8%. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

We propose and evaluate slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols designed to mitigate narrowband interference, introducing a specific throughput metric to assess their performance. Our analysis of slotted ALOHA examines interference probability and throughput relative to system parameters, revealing behaviors distinct from traditional wireless networks; notably, when packets contain multiple chirps, higher transmission rates can result in lower interference probabilities. Furthermore, we define Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) as a sensing component of our CSMA proposal, characterizing both success and failure events where transmission occurs only upon successful CCA. We analyze CCA success rates, interference likelihood, and throughput across varying parameters, observing that, contrary to wireless standards, maximizing attempt rates can optimize throughput in specific scenarios. Extensive simulations validate our analytical findings and compare the two protocols, demonstrating that CSMA consistently outperforms slotted ALOHA in realistic network conditions. Finally, we outline potential future research directions for FMCW radar networks, specifically mentioning adaptive FMCW and MAC protocols. This work builds upon and expands the findings presented in our previous conference publication.

This document extends the research previously reported in reference [1]. That work analyzed and compared slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols for single- and multiuser FMCW radar systems, with this paper focusing exclusively on extending the multiuser discussion. The extension incorporates more detailed examinations of transmission attempt success, interference probability, and throughput, while also addressing scenarios where not all radars utilize every available time slot. As with the prior work, the core finding remains that CSMA generally offers higher throughput than slotted ALOHA, though there exist specific situations where allowing radars to attempt transmission regardless of CSMA status can be beneficial. The detailed analysis in [1] was constrained by the assumption that all radars employed the exact same parameters; this work removes that restriction to create a more practical multiuser model. Additionally, detailed calculations from [1] regarding general multiuser cases where some radars do not use all time slots were skipped; this paper provides those detailed analyses. Although the detailed study in [1] assumed equal packet sizes, the detailed work in this paper remains valid for scenarios where all radars transmit packets of equal but arbitrary size.

Building on the success of tensor decomposition in modeling entity-relation interactions within static knowledge graphs, we introduce Time-LowFER, a parameter-efficient and time-aware extension of the LowFER low-rank tensor factorization model. Addressing existing limitations in temporal representation, we propose a model-agnostic, cycle-aware time-encoding scheme that provides a more generalized view of time. These methods are integrated into a unified framework for temporal knowledge graph embedding, with a specific focus on processing time-sensitive data. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach performs competitively with, and in some cases surpasses, state-of-the-art semantic matching models across two benchmarks. To prove the efficacy of temporal representations in handling factual data, an inference task is performed on two standard benchmarks using various state-of-the-art methods, with our proposed approach achieving the best results. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of the performance of static versus temporal graph representations is conducted. The findings of this research are freely accessible via the arXiv preprint at https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02852.

scientific and engineering fields, including power grids, gene regulatory networks, social and financial networks, and astronomy. In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering is often unfeasible. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly account for their temporal evolution. This paper introduces a novel methodology for clustering dynamic systems directly from time-series data, inherently capturing the system's dynamical behavior. Specifically, we define a distance metric between system trajectories and utilize it to cluster time-series data over a specified time interval. We demonstrate that this approach minimizes the variance of the distance metric both inter-cluster and intra-cluster, thereby ensuring that system trajectories are closer to one another within the same cluster than to those in other clusters. To facilitate computation, we employ K-means clustering, which enables the derivation of an analytical expression for the gradient of the objective function. This allows K-means to be implemented as a gradient-based algorithm for clustering dynamic systems via their time-series data. The proposed method is validated on two distinct dynamic system models: the Lorenz attractor and actual wind turbine time-series data. We conclude by proposing future directions for research. This study demonstrates that dynamic systems can be effectively clustered based on their behavioral differences using the introduced distance metric, even when data is available without mathematical models. Consequently, the findings of this work are relevant to a wide range of applications, including climate modeling, control theory, telecommunications, and the analysis of dynamic complex networks. By enabling the classification of dynamic system behaviors directly from time-series data, the proposed approach holds significant potential for clustering the types, roles, and behaviors of complex network nodes. This functionality could enhance the analysis, monitoring, and maintenance of power grids, gas distribution networks, communication networks, and similar dynamic network structures. Additionally, the work contributes to the broader goal of identifying patterns and structures within data. We also note that the clustering of dynamical systems via their trajectories has been examined in prior studies; however, those works often rely on mathematical models or assume linear system dynamics. In contrast, the proposed method addresses the data-driven clustering of dynamic system trajectories without requiring mathematical models, even when the systems exhibit nonlinear behavior.

Current approaches often struggle with unreliable gradient estimates or inaccurate sentence representations. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN, which produces sparse, semantically interpretable sentence representations for the discriminator. The core mechanism involves treating an embedding matrix as a dictionary, approximating the generator's output feature representation at each time step through a linear combination of a minimal number of selected word embeddings. These semantic-rich representations not only minimize unnecessary noise to facilitate efficient adversarial training but also render the entire process fully differentiable. Empirical results across various text generation datasets demonstrate performance gains, particularly in sequence-level metrics like BLEU. Furthermore, we utilize the derived sparse representations to compute semantic similarity between sentences, effectively replacing conventional semantic similarity metrics in supervised GAN training. Both training and inference are significantly accelerated through the employment of an attention mechanism. Experimental evidence confirms that our method not only delivers superior overall performance but also enhances the local sensitivity of the discriminator.

To evaluate the detectability of this phenomenon, we constructed a mathematical model incorporating key variables such as microbial survival duration, stellar velocity dispersion, and ejecta dispersion. Our analysis indicates that the statistical pair-distribution function, representing correlations between life-bearing systems, could serve as a viable diagnostic tool for interstellar panspermia, specifically when ejecta velocity dispersion exceeds stellar dispersion. By offering heuristic estimates of model parameters across different astrophysical settings, we conclude that open and globular clusters are the most promising environments for testing the feasibility of interstellar panspermia. Most significantly, we identify a hypothetical "biotic globular cluster" as the definitive target for confirming this hypothesis. To create this scenario, we must first rule out endogenous life generation on individual stars and demonstrate vertical migration of life-capable systems toward the cluster core. We propose that multi-epoch astrometric data from the Gaia mission, combined with very large aperture imaging telescopes, will be instrumental in investigating the vertical migration of stars within open clusters and establishing the biotic globular cluster hypothesis. Finally, we discuss how future missions, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory, the Overcam Observatory, and sample-return technologies, could search for microbial life on planetary satellites or robustly test endogenous biosynthesis, thereby either confirming or disproving interstellar panspermia. This paper is accompanied by a associated web resource. To exclude endogenous life synthesis, we recommend focusing on old, single-star, low-metallicity, and isolated stellar systems, ideally located on the main sequence or red giant branch, as the most viable targets for demonstrating that life did not arise natively.

This framework posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, triggering a sequence of subsequent symmetry violations at lower energies driven by minor mixings between levels. We introduce a straightforward model where this concept is implemented through scalar portals that facilitate small inter-level mixing. Within this approach, the significant disparity between energy scales—such as those of the Planck and electroweak realms—emerges from the cumulative product of several small factors related to these mixing coefficients. Furthermore, dark matter fields may arise in this scenario from matter fields situated at one or multiple intermediate energy levels between the maximum and minimum scales. Finally, we examine the constraints imposed by current experimental data, including those from colliders, neutron electric dipole moments, and dark matter direct detection experiments. Our analysis indicates that the simplest model configurations face restrictions, with the most stringent limits stemming from collider and dark matter detection experiments, whereas the scenario involving intermediate mixing presents significantly looser constraints. \textit{Note added in proof:} Following the submission of this article, a number of studies have been published that further investigate situations analogous to the present work; these works are cited in Reference 34.

We propose that the baryon asymmetry of the universe (BAU) originates from baryogenesis at multiple energy scales, specifically through the mixing of fundamental matter fields at distinct levels. Within this multi-scale framework, the vast differences between energy regimes—such as those between the electroweak and Planck energies—are explained by the nonlinear amplification of intrinsically small mixing coefficients. We formulate a simple two-level model where matter mixing induces a hierarchy of scales and demonstrate how this accounts for both the BAU and the existence of dark matter. Additionally, we explore scenarios where dark matter emerges directly from this multi-scale structure and show how the asymmetry in dark matter abundance can be generated simultaneously with the BAU. Our proposed simplest two-level setup involves the intermediate mixing between the GUT and Planck scales, which offers very limited constraints compared to traditional single-scale models. Extending this to three or more levels introduces additional possibilities for generating the BAU and dark matter, though these extensions are subject to stricter limitations, such as those imposed by the muon $g-2$ anomaly.

For over four decades, researchers have employed the functional response to characterize how predation rates respond to changes in prey density. While field estimates of functional responses remain challenging, they are essential for testing predictions derived from optimal foraging theory. This study utilizes high-frequency radio-telemetry data from a top predator, the gray wolf (*Canis lupus*), to estimate a type II functional response from observations made within a defined prey density range. Findings indicate that the functional response of gray wolves to white-tailed deer (*Odocoileus virginianus*) is best modeled as a combination of a type II response at lower prey densities and a type I response at higher densities. These results hold significant implications for managing prey species and their habitats, as well as for refining movement models used in wildlife impact assessments.

Traditional analyses of these phenomena often rely on the eigenvector of the adjacency or inverse Hessian matrices, typically requiring additional metrics to evaluate the intensity of the phenomenon. In this study, we utilize the generalized eigenvector (PSD) method, originally proposed to identify multiple co-existing local communities, to directly quantify the intensity of localization without relying on supplementary measures. We examine diverse systems including random and scale-free networks, homogeneous and gradient lattices, driving-free and driven quantum systems, and periodic potentials. The findings demonstrate that PSD is capable of both detecting and measuring localization effects where other indicators can only confirm their occurrence. Furthermore, we show that, similar to the ability of PSD to uncover multiple co-existing communities, localization intensity can also exist in multiple co-existing states. Finally, we find that on gradient lattices, PSD intensity follows a specific distribution law when the system undergoes a transition from delocalized to localized states. We expect PSD to be applicable to other instances of localization, particularly in complex systems where heterogeneity is intrinsic. We anticipate that this work will encourage the investigation of location phenomena across a broader range of complex systems.

In many branches of physics, particularly statistical mechanics, entropy is extensively employed to characterize the macroscopic behavior of complex systems. We demonstrate that for systems exhibiting localization, the entropy—defined either microscopically or macroscopically—becomes negative. This observation holds true for both discrete systems, such as quantum quantum walks on uniform lattices, and continuous systems, such as quantum states in periodic potentials. We argue that negative entropy serves as a direct and universal indicator of limited state activity within a system, offering a fresh perspective on the underlying mechanism of location. We anticipate that this finding will stimulate further research into location phenomena throughout physics and other fields dealing with complex systems. Additionally, we expect this work to aid in identifying and quantifying such phenomena in areas where they have yet to be explored.

Our analysis covers transitions in quantum phase transitions, such as Anderson and localization transitions in quantum quantum walks, as well as Anderson transitions in continuous states. We also examine the Ehrenfest transition regarding energy density in an ideal Bose gas and critical phenomena in the synergetics of complex systems. While previous research has attempted to assess football defense by forecasting ball gains and attacks based on player and ball positions, these studies overlooked event significance, assumed flawless tracking of all 22 players, and neglected the impact of diversity factors such as nationality and gender. Table legends and captions often fail to convey the full context of figures, hindering comprehension for visually impaired readers or non-native English speakers. To address this, we present VisuAria, an interactive web tool that generates natural language descriptions for scientific visualizations using diverse natural language generation models. VisuAria allows users to customize inputs by selecting from various contextual sources, including image features, data values, and parameter settings, while choosing from multiple NLP models and architectures. It also incorporates an external text API, the Languaage Model as a Service framework, to support remote inference. The VisuAria website is available at https://noah-schulz.github.io/VisuAria/. Supplementary materials, featuring additional demonstrations of VisuARia's capabilities and benchmarks of included text models, can be found at https://noah-schulz.github.io/VisuAria_Supplementary/.

Video understanding remains a major challenge in computer vision, and while deep learning has enhanced performance on clean data, it struggles with real-world images containing deformations, occlusions, and other distortions. Current solutions often require large quantities of training data for each specific 3D object of interest, a requirement that is impractical when only a single object is visible. We introduce a unified network capable of generating 3D line measurements from both clean and distorted images containing a single object. By incorporating a shape prior into an end-to-end deep learning framework, our method achieves accurate results even with only a few clean training samples. Our experiments across various objects and types of distortions show that we significantly exceed the performance of current state-of-the-art formulators.

In contrast, many control tasks involve similar but distinct dynamics that can be effectively represented as a latent variable. We propose Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a framework that defines a family of related dynamical systems using a low-dimensional set of latent factors. This approach offers a straightforward and efficient method for learning and performing inference on this Gaussian graphical model without relying on approximations such as variational inference. Our results demonstrate that HiP-RSSMs surpass both standard RSSMs and competing multi-task models across various demanding robotic benchmarks, including both physical systems and simulations. Furthermore, we show that the framework can capture diverse dynamics by observing just a few short trajectories, enabling accurate prediction on new tasks after observing only a single short sequence. Finally, we utilize HiP-RSSMs to investigate the connection between related systems and observation adequacy, revealing that these models can identify regions of ambiguous dynamics caused by sensor noise and limited observation ranges, thereby providing insights into why certain dynamics are easily learned while others are not.

We observe that high-dimensional datasets often consist of a small number of underlying factors that can be captured by a latent graph. This paper introduces Graph factor analysis (GRA), the first model capable of simultaneously learning these latent factors and the structure of the data. We demonstrate that HiP-RSSMs exceed both conventional RSSMs and competing multi-task models on several difficult robotic problems, ranging from physical hardware to simulators. Additionally, our work reveals how to specify a prior over dynamically similar tasks to optimize data efficiency. We further illustrate how HiP-RSSMs can capture a range of related dynamics based on observed data alone, eliminating the need for explicit model specification. The study also explores how limited data can yield accurate predictions for newly observed, yet similar, systems.

While various approaches commonly measure polarization in social networks by examining their structure alone, we evaluated eight such methods and found that all produce high polarization scores even for random networks sharing the density and degree distributions of real-world networks. Collaborative filtering (CF) typically relies on explicit user feedback, which is time-consuming to obtain. Although recent methods utilize implicit implicit implicit feedback by analyzing user behavior, they often struggle with data sparsity. We introduce a novel approach that learns to convert sparse implicit feedback into dense explicit feedback, enabling the use of effective explicit CF techniques. Unlike implicit feedback, which is sparse, our method is dense and rich in information.
Nodes within a network often possess attributes that can be analyzed to uncover hidden patterns. For instance, political accounts on Twitter can be identified by the topics they discuss. We examine the normalization of numerical data on social networks, a step crucial for tasks like clustering and classification. Although clustering methods for attribute-rich nodes have implicit feedback applications, this paper concentrates on classification. We analyze image data, specifically the 20 newsgroups dataset, which was collected to help users identify spam. We investigate multiple clustering algorithms for this data, clustering posts based on their text, and subsequently testing image-based methods to classify the resulting clusters as spam or ham. We then assess these methods' performance using implicit feedback derived from user behavior.

While this method offers a more realistic and comprehensive representation compared to single-layer networks, it simultaneously introduces inherent complexities in system analysis. In this work, we present a method to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by utilizing the join of matrices that encode both intra-layer and inter-layer connections. This strategy yields a "reduced" representation of the original multilayer system that exhibits equivalent dynamics. By solving for the reduced system and propagating these solutions back to the full network, we can determine system states. Furthermore, applying this same approach allows us to derive sufficient conditions for the stability of synchronous solutions, accounting for the influence of inter-layer interactions on the stability of within-layer dynamics. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that the primary characteristic governing the stability of synchronous states in multilayer Kuramoto oscillators is the sum of the weights of intra-layer and inter-layer interaction matrices. Our proposed technique not only enhances the analysis of multilayer network dynamics but also extends to other systems with similar representable structures. (LessMore...)

If ${\cal{D}}$ is involutive, this method yields a sequence of successive first-order involutive operators ${\cal{D}}_1, ... , {\cal{D}}_n$ for a ground manifold of dimension $n$. In contrast, the "inverse problem," which is more challenging, seeks an operator ${\cal{D}}: \xi \rightarrow \eta$ that produces a specified generating CC ${\cal{D}}_1\eta=0$. When feasible—specifically when the differential module defined by ${\cal{D}}_1$ is torsion-free—we state that ${\cal{D}}_1$ is parametrized by ${\cal{D}}$. Generally, no specific relationship exists between ${\cal{D}}$ and ${\cal{D}}_2$. The parametrization is termed "minimum" if the differential module associated with ${\cal{D}}$ possesses a vanishing differential rank, thereby forming a torsion module. The parametrization is "complete" if every solution of ${\cal{D}}_1\eta=0$ can be represented as $\eta=\psi(\xi)$ for some $\xi$, implying that ${\cal{D}}$ is surjective. Typically, both minimum and complete parametrizations are unique up to equivalence. This letter introduces a parametrization that is neither minimum nor complete; however, it enables the derivation of both the minimum and complete parametrizations through algebraic manipulation. This non-optimal approach finds application in constructing the Schur complement and represents a crucial step toward a canonical decomposition. Although not entirely novel, the proposed method offers a fresh perspective. It should be noted, though, that this specific approach does not apply to parametrizing the differential equation $y_{xx}=y^2$. For that specific case, one must employ a minimum parametrization, potentially combined with additional constraints.

Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error.

Correcting errors is fundamentally distinct from specifying them; the space of potential corrections is considerably more complex than the space of test outcomes, a challenge that becomes even more pronounced in geometric theory because tests function as proofs. Consequently, our error specification requires defining a new proof technique termed "test reflexivity." This approach defines errors as irreducible paths of quadratic betweenness relations among the logical rules and axioms of the testing environment. We establish a test reflexivity theorem within natural deduction extended by test formation rules, demonstrating how to derive any such irreducible path from the extended rules. Furthermore, we explore strategies for populating a database of error specifications, including methods for suggesting corrections based on examined paths and locating existing open problems in mathematics and computer science.

In addition to these theoretical contributions, we have built a practical environment for specifying and displaying stick diagrams. It is important to note that these contributions represent a subset of errors; not all errors can be characterized by stick diagrams, and some are more tractable. For instance, missing case distinctions in case analysis can be addressed directly through type error extensions, while incorrect applications of if-then-else constructs constitute standard first-order errors. Similarly, applying functions with mismatched argument types to arguments of the wrong kind can be handled without special treatment, as can applying functions to too few or too many arguments, a feature already present in Haskell.

Errors that are neither particularly difficult nor rare typically involve applying a function of type A -> B to an argument of type C where C is not equivalent to A. These are the errors our tool is specifically designed to detect, as they are the only ones for which the space of corrections cannot be easily explored. These "geometric" errors are among the most prevalent, since almost every function application offers the possibility of such a mistake.

In this work, we investigate the application of HyperNetworks to create hyper-prompts, introducing HyperPrompt—a new architecture designed for task-conditioning self-attention within Transformers using prompt-based methods. These hyper-prompts are end-to-endly learned by a HyperNetwork, enabling the system to learn multiple tasks simultaneously without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. By acting as memory hooks, HyperPrompt facilitates the direct retrieval of intermediate states from various layers and positions across the Transformer, thereby activating implicit task knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompt achieves performance competitive with full fine-tuning on tasks including machine translation, summarization, text QA, and language modeling, while also delivering strong results on few-shot natural language inference. Furthermore, HyperPrompt significantly reduces training costs, offering up to an order of magnitude decrease in both training time and parameters compared to full fine-tuning. Finally, we present HyperPrompt Visualizer, the first method to explicitly visualize how HyperPrompt supports task execution. This tool allows for the simultaneous examination of learned hyper-prompts and memory hooks through distinct visual representations, revealing diverse patterns of task knowledge stored within the Transformer's implicit memory. We release all code to support this work. In summary, HyperPrompt serves as a unified framework that learns prompts via HyperNetworks from multiple tasks, delivering state-of-the-art results on few-shot CLUTRR and effectively activating implicit knowledge across a broad spectrum of NLP tasks. We release code and models for all experiments. We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes possess complete awareness of the network's state at every step—including all random choices—unlimited computational capabilities, and the freedom to deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. Our primary contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estimating network size despite a high volume of Byzantine nodes. Specifically, this algorithm accurately estimates the size of sparse, small-world expander networks containing up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ represents the unknown network size and $\delta$ is any fixed positive constant. The algorithm produces a constant-factor estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability, ensuring that a large majority ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction) of honest nodes obtain the correct network size. Furthermore, the approach is fully distributed, lightweight, and easy to implement; it completes in $O(\log^3{n})$ rounds, utilizes small messages per round, and imposes minimal local computational costs on each node. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $\log^3{n}$ round complexity is optimal up to constant factors for achieving constant-factor network size estimates in such environments. Beyond handling a high quantity of Byzantine nodes, our method is particularly suited for low-power devices with constrained memory and bandwidth, networks exhibiting small constant degree, and scenarios where the overall network size is not exponentially larger than the count of Byzantine nodes. In contrast to related approaches, our solution avoids heavy computational complexities, probabilistic assumptions regarding random choice distributions (beyond minimally fair coin flips), direct network scanning, or reliance on synchronous communication. Unlike traditional approaches, this method avoids linearizations and parametric assumptions about downstream traffic conditions or vehicle dynamics; instead, it relies on a "good driver" hypothesis. Traffic signal optimization, often achieved through adaptive control systems, depends on real-time data regarding approaching and downstream queue lengths. While camera-based methods are effective where installable, their high costs limit deployment to small urban areas, making them impossible to widespread install. In contrast, probe vehicle data offers a low-cost alternative. Although existing techniques can estimate these metrics from probe data, they frequently depend on parametric models, which can introduce errors when conditions deviate from model specifications. This paper introduces a screening step to select an optimal, optimally identifiable parametric copula distribution from a broad class of copulas. Subsequently, a dimension reduction step is detailed. This reduction is critical to minimize estimation cost and ensure that the high-dimensional traffic process can be accurately reconstructed from the lower-dimensional data.

We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. This strategy circumvents the challenges associated with ensuring the Casimir invariant of the constraint's elliptic operator remains positive. To implement this, we employ a standard gradient method combined with a standard solver for the resulting system of linear equations. We have developed a standard CTT constraint solver using this technique, which we demonstrate is both stable and efficient on cylindrical and Schwarzschild spacetimes with various matter configurations, including those with boundaries. Notably, the method proves highly efficient when paired with standard multigrid solvers for the linear system, offering significant advantages for space-time initialization, particularly when the conformal factor exhibits steep gradients, as occurs near matter boundaries. Potential extensions to other initial value problem solutions, such as those in gravitational wave generation, are discussed. Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites represent an emerging class of materials that display diverse properties driven by their intricate electronic band structures and magnetic ordering. Although the net Berry curvature vanishes due to time-reversal symmetry, slight displacements from the high-symmetry point generate a significant localized contribution. Recent years have seen BERT and similar models dominate information retrieval benchmarks. To deploy such high-performing yet computationally expensive models efficiently, we utilize lighter architectures like DistBERT through knowledge distillation. Building on prior work that demonstrated strong offline and real-world results, we further enhance performance by incorporating label information and implementing spatial-batchwise distillation, reducing latency by more than 50%. Additionally, we present the first end-to-end evaluation of BERT-based distillation in a real-world commercial online experiment involving over 200 million users, showing that even small improvements in document quality can yield significant gains. These findings provide a comprehensive guide for future search and ranking efforts.

for the discovery and characterization of novel functional materials. Recent advancements in automation and experimental methodologies have accelerated these measurements and enhanced their resolution, resulting in massive datasets requiring analysis. These improvements are especially notable at user facilities and synchrotron light sources. Although machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly utilized to process and interpret large data volumes in real time, significant hurdles remain: the general user community often lacks ML expertise, and deploying ML models presents technical challenges. In this work, we showcase several representative ML models designed for the rapid analysis of large-scale synchrotron X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) data. We provide an overview of model selection, development, and deployment within a production environment. To address the needs of non-experts, we implemented a Python package featuring a unified API for selecting models, input and output formatting, and managing deployment-specific tasks such as error handling and machine usage. The ML models and this package are freely accessible on GitHub, enabling the customization of APIs, the introduction of new models, and their deployment in production settings. The developed API supports a broad range of applications, including real-time experimentation guidance, the creation of visually appealing figures for publications, and database population. We specifically focus on deploying ML models at beamline 8.3.1 at the Advanced Light Source to illustrate the benefits and challenges of utilizing ML in high-throughput experimental environments. The presented API simplifies machine learning workflows, making these processes more accessible to the general scientific community.

Recent advancements in automated experimentation have enabled the rapid generation of extensive datasets, creating both opportunities and challenges for determining material properties through machine learning (ML). To facilitate these efforts, we have developed an open-source library for experimental ML that supports various ML algorithms, from simple to complex models. This library streamlines the configuration, execution, and deployment of models to analyze data during experiments. Its key features include support for multiple algorithms, a user-friendly interface for configuring hyperparameters, and the ability to output results in formats compatible with control systems for real-time experimentation. To validate its utility, we applied this library to deploy models for analyzing time-domain transmission data measuring metal skin depth. Validated on hardware at beamline 8.3.1 at the Advanced Light Source (LBNL), this library is freely available on GitHub, offering a crucial step toward conducting high-throughput experiments with embedded machine learning.

To accelerate the characterization of materials at automated beamlines, it is necessary to develop frameworks for machine learning (ML) that can process data in real time.

approach to solving combinatorial optimization problems by embedding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian. This paper derives the Dinosaur (DIN) mapping, a novel encoding scheme for quadratic binary optimization (QBO) into an Ising Hamiltonian. Unlike the standard quadratic Ising mapping (SIM), the DIN mapping guarantees that the energy of an excited state arising from a single bit-flip error scales with the problem's size, whereas DIN energies for all other excited states are constant and independent of problem dimensions. Theoretically, these properties make QA using the DIN mapping significantly more resilient to both experimental noise and noiseless deformed Hamiltonians, such as those caused by Hamiltonian evolution under external perturbations. Numerically, we evaluate the DIN mapping against SIM on a specific class of random quadratic binary forms within a specific noise model, demonstrating that DIN maintains an energy gap that does not decline as problem size increases, similar to uns noisy excited states. These findings suggest that the DIN mapping could enhance the solving of larger problems on current and near-future quantum annealers, which suffer from limited connectivity, sparse interactions, and noise. Finally, we examine a scenario where the energy of all excited states not guaranteed to scale must be handled, showing how to process them within a specific solution threshold in a polynomial amount of time relative to the problem's size. The paper also addresses various other aspects, including states with multiple bit flips, connectivity, connectivity-efficient transformations to equivalent Hamiltonians, comparisons with other mapping schemes, and extensions to spin-systems with $S>1/2$. The paper is accompanied by supplementary material addressing additional topics like numerical comparisons, random quadratic forms, pre- and post-annealing, and finite-temperature effects.

In many practical machine learning scenarios, the data volume or feature dimension exceeds the memory capacity of a single computer, necessitating either data-parallel or model-parallel architectures. Although model-parallelism offers distinct advantages, such as potentially higher accuracy and the ability to process massive datasets impossible for a single machine, it currently suffers from slower training speeds and longer time-to-solution compared to data-parallel methods. We propose utilizing model-parallelism for medium-scale problems to achieve solution quality unattainable otherwise, without sacrificing efficiency or requiring additional memory per computer. Our data shows that this strategy not only yields solutions of superior quality but also does so more efficiently.

We address large-scale non-convex optimization problems arising in machine learning, where finding a solution of acceptable accuracy within a reasonable duration is challenging. We analyze two typical cases: training deep neural networks (DNNs) and solving $l_0$-regularized regression for sparse signal recovery. To overcome the limitations of conventional model-parallelization, we develop a novel parallel algorithm. The core component is a new parallel estimator designed to calculate gradient approximations more accurately and efficiently than traditional local gradient estimators. This allows memory constraints to be relaxed and scaling to be achieved without increasing communication overhead. We establish both non-asymptotic convergence rates and solution accuracy for problems with limited data. Experimental results confirm that our method outperforms existing data-parallel and model-parallel techniques.

This study investigates how nanofillers influence the microstructure and mechanical properties of epoxy matrices filled with glass fibers. Specifically, we examine the synergistic effects of graphene and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) on these properties. By systematically varying the concentrations of both nanofillers, we determine their optimal levels and evaluate how these additives affect the formation and characteristics of epoxy-rich phases at interfaces. Furthermore, we observe an anomalous anomalous concentration dependence of the composite's mechanical properties, which is attributed to an anomalous concentration dependence of the specific surface area of the epoxy-rich phases, a phenomenon not previously reported. Additionally, we address an apparent contradiction between the improved specific toughness at the fiber-matrix interface and the reduced specific toughness (both isotropic and anisotropic) of the overall composite. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for enhancing the mechanical performance of fiber-reinforced composite materials.

In various fiber-reinforced composite systems, a severe trade-off exists between toughness and anisotropy. While the presence of a nanofiller network can improve the specific toughness at the fiber-matrix interface, it often leads to a reduction in the bulk material's toughness and an increased anisotropy.

We developed a theoretical model to explain the formation of a percolating nanofiller network within the epoxy-rich phases at the interfaces of fiber-reinforced composites. This network accounts for the material's specific mechanical properties and resolves the conflict between interfacial and bulk toughness. Experimental data on the microstructure and concentration dependence of these networks support the validity of our model.

While numerous studies have identified factors influencing blood pressure variability, few have examined how personality traits affect these fluctuations. This work investigates the impact of the Big Five traits—neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness—on both short-term and long-term blood pressure fluctuations. Using data from 1,709 participants in the Whitehall II study, we found that higher neuroticism correlates with increased blood pressure variability, a finding that held true after controlling for confounding variables like demographics, lifestyle, and brain structure. Conversely, greater conscientiousness was linked to both elevated mean blood pressure and heightened variability. In contrast, no significant associations were detected for the other three Big Five traits. These results carry important implications for assessing cardiovascular risk and designing personalized healthcare strategies.

We address the task of maintaining equilibrium in uncertain dynamical systems subject to constraints on both states and controls. This problem is relevant to aerial vehicles, mobile robots, flight through obstacle-laden environments, adaptive control, and more. The methodology relies on minimizing a Hamiltonian function derived from two dynamical model estimates and the system's cost function. These models are acquired through exploration; however, the amount of data needed for accurate learning in localized regions allows the use of a conservative update policy. Such a policy prevents violations of state and control constraints, as well as the original dynamical model, while also safeguarding against overfitting.

By focusing on an ontology of non-classical sets that is both accessible and practically applicable, our method resolves many challenges faced by prior formalization efforts. We propose the axiomatic system BZFC, which is derived by carefully translating ZFC axioms into this four-valued framework. The pursuit of multiple models for set-theoretic axioms has long been possible through the standard model-theoretic approach, which relies on the classical two-valued logic of either being true or false. However, the "set-theoretic universe" can alternatively be modeled using non-classical multi-valued logics. This paper aims to establish a "non-classical" set theory, termed QZFC, by translating the classical ZFC axioms into a four-valued logic framework. We demonstrate that the "classicality" axiom, which affirms the existence of classical sets, is sufficient to generate the entire set-theoretic universe non-classically. Furthermore, the concept of non-classicality within the object language finds a direct mirror in the meta-theory. Specifically, assertions of classicality, truth, or falsity regarding non-classical sets in the object language correspond to the "trueness" of the same properties within the meta-theory. Consequently, the "classicality" axiom in QZFC effectively encapsulates the completeness of the non-classical set-theoretic universe.

Previous studies have focused on classifying specific actions, such as swinging a racket or lifting a weight, by leveraging neural data. However, these efforts have not addressed the prediction of performance accuracy, a critical factor for enhancing an athlete's posture and preventing errors. This paper introduces a system capable of forecasting EEG signals when a subject performs incorrect movements. By predicting misjudgments, the proposed approach can facilitate improvements in posture and accuracy. To achieve this, we gathered EEG data from three individuals executing two distinct actions. EEG signals were recorded while participants performed either an "up" movement, correctly lifting a weight, or an "incorrect" movement, failing to lift it. A decoding module was then constructed based on the neural data obtained during these incorrect movements. The accuracy of this module, which was trained on neural patterns associated with faulty execution, effectively predicted the user's ability to lift the weight, achieving a classification accuracy of 75%.

Consequently, this paper proposes an implementation framework for security within big data mining and discusses its potential applications in vertical markets, such as government and defense sectors. By utilizing this framework, stakeholders can evaluate the feasibility of implementing big data security in specific contexts, thereby facilitating easier adoption and contributing to global security and stability. The proposed mining security framework has been successfully tested in government-related data security scenarios, with its principles and implementations being straightforward enough to be adapted for other vertical markets. Such implementation would open up significant opportunities within the global big data security market. Ultimately, this paper serves as a reference for both the implementation of security in big data systems and the horizontal expansion of big data security markets.

These topological Anderson insulators are defined by a disorder-induced transition electric dipole moment. Furthermore, the localization length within these topological Anderson insulators displays a non-monotonic variation with changing binary disorder strength. Consequently, developing rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling faulty syndrome measurements is essential. This study demonstrates that decoding these codes within a full fault-tolerant framework can be naturally recast as repeated interactions between a decoder and its environment, enabling the application of reinforcement learning to train decoding agents. As a proof of concept, we utilized deep Q-learning to create fast decoding agents for the surface code across various noise models. Although surface code agents exhibit slightly lower performance in continuous noise environments, they remain competitive with current surface code decode agents. Additionally, we analyzed the connection between the error correction capabilities of these agents and the properties of the underlying quantum channel. The code, framework, and analysis presented are essential components of comprehensive, adaptable decoding solutions required for the coming era of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

Although this technique offers several advantages over standard quantum evolution, a key limitation is that the amount of extractable information from the quantum jumps alone is typically insufficient. To overcome this, we introduce a hybrid approach that integrates discontinuous quantum jumps with the continuous unitary time evolution of the quantum state. This method enables the extraction of more information regarding the parameter than would be possible through the quantum jumps alone. We demonstrate that the estimated parameter can be determined with higher accuracy by analyzing either the sequence of observed quantum jumps, the continuity of the unitary evolution, or a combination of both. In both cases, we determine that the hybrid method can achieve an estimation precision that approaches the ultimate quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound. Additionally, we illustrate that this approach is particularly well-suited for implementation within a quantum circuit architecture utilizing trapped ions.
Measurement precision in quantum metrology can be enhanced through two main strategies: utilizing highly entangled states before a single-shot measurement, or encoding information into the temporal pattern of repeated measurements on a quantum state. While the former is often theoretically optimal, it remains practically unfeasible for any state of significant size. The latter approach, which we term "quantum jump metrology," allows information to be encoded into the sequences of discontinuous quantum jumps from which estimates can be derived. To further improve precision and extract additional information, we propose a hybrid version of quantum jump metrology. Nevertheless, despite comparable computational resources between cloud and on-premise HPC environments, their network architectures and performance characteristics can diverge substantially. For instance, the use of distinct network transport and routing protocols in these systems may generate network noise, potentially constraining application scalability. This study examines the network performance, scalability, and economic implications of executing HPC tasks on cloud platforms. The research begins with detailed small-scale measurements focusing on latency, bandwidth, and collective communication patterns, followed by large-scale network performance simulations. Validated across four major cloud providers and three on-premise HPC systems, the findings demonstrate that both network and operating system noise can significantly affect performance and costs at various scales. When cloud providers do not apply noise premiums, executed costs can exceed on-premise alternatives due to elevated noise-induced timeouts. Additionally, the simulations identify suitable strategies for noise mitigation, which can reduce executed costs by up to 50% relative to unmitigated scenarios. Ultimately, this work provides essential insights for accurately estimating noise effects in combined cloud and on-premise settings and for developing applications capable of efficient execution across these platforms. Finally, a companion paper addresses the in-depth performance modeling and simulation methodologies employed in this study.

Cloud computing serves as a potent solution for running diverse scientific and enterprise HPC tasks, particularly those demanding temporary, substantial resources, flexible scheduling, and monitoring. However, as both cloud and on-premise HPC platforms rely on shared hardware foundations, the transition to clouds can introduce performance pitfalls stemming from underlying infrastructure issues or noise, such as network interference. Recent studies have examined noise-induced performance losses, often reporting up to 99.9% reductions in strong scaling, a finding that is especially alarming given that these losses can persist even when applications receive identical network bandwidth. This extreme performance degradation can lead to significantly higher actual costs than anticipated, as the "per second" price of computed performance can surge into the thousands, potentially surpassing the value of the results themselves. Consequently, users must consider not only financial pricing but also the performance implications of where and how their work is executed. This paper presents findings from investigating noise in real-world forecasts for computational weather predictions performed on actual cloud and on-premise HPC platforms. These observations highlight the challenges of running HPC workloads in clouds, underscore the necessity of incorporating performance (alongside cost) into workflow management for multi-user, multi-scale tasks, and suggest potential strategies for mitigating noise. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central server holding the reward function and can interact with it only a fixed number of times per round due to severe resource constraints. # I. Introduction

Learning in wireless or distributed environments presents a particularly demanding extension of the standard decision-theoretic model, where a central entity iteratively observes an input $x_t$, selects an action $s_t$, receives a reward $y_t$, and updates its policy for future iterations. In this setup, a single point of failure can render the entire system useless, a vulnerability exacerbated when the learned model is an expensive, black-box function. This paper focuses on a more robust and widely applicable model where both the input and reward are observed locally by a single point, and the selected action is the sole information transmitted to a central server holding the reward function.
