This study employs a two-phase methodology: the first phase utilizes a survey of 22 Agile professionals from the general public to identify key differences between hybrid and fully remote work environments, while the second phase deeply examines 16 case studies drawn from the tech industry. The findings reveal that fully remote work significantly increases the time required for asynchronous communication compared to hybrid settings and drastically heightens the reliance on team autonomy. Furthermore, the impact of remote work on Agile processes and outcomes varies widely across different organizations and even between individual teams within the same company. Ultimately, the study concludes that the suitability of specific Agile processes and the resulting success are heavily influenced by the immediate local context of each individual team.

Over the last decade, numerous studies have investigated the influence of Scrum on software development success, yet their approaches to defining and measuring success have lacked standardization. To clarify existing literature and guide future work, this paper systematically reviews successful Scrum implementations by first surveying the field to categorize various definitions of success and identify the metrics used to assess them in software development. The discussion highlights the benefits and limitations of these different success frameworks and offers recommendations for selecting an appropriate framework for both hybrid and fully remote work settings.

In adopting Scrum, the choice of process is often a matter of individual team discretion, yet the factors influencing this decision remain unclear. This paper explores the criteria that guide Agile process selection in distributed work scenarios and how they differ between hybrid and fully remote contexts. Additionally, the suitable processes vary based on the nature of the software work, the level of team autonomy, and the availability of on-site on-shore developers.

The challenge of remotely estimating story points was identified as a significant issue in previous literature. This paper analyzes the reasons behind remote estimation difficulties and discusses strategies for overcoming them.

Although the relationship between team autonomy and software quality varies by organization, fully remote work significantly reduces the time available for actual development, substantially lowering team capacity. Consequently, teams must either decrease the scope of their responsibilities or increase autonomy to deliver the necessary features.

Prior studies have overlooked the impact of remote work on software architects. Research indicates that distributed work can lead to fragmented mental models of the system, potentially resulting in suboptimal architectural decisions. Furthermore, the consequences of such decisions can be especially severe in large systems, as the time needed to repair them grows exponentially with size.

Automatically generating taxonomic hierarchies from unstructured data is a pivotal yet challenging task with numerous applications, such as organizing news feeds, categorizing web pages, and structuring research publications. These insights are crucial for both humans and machines navigating large-scale information networks. Recent advancements have produced various models for hierarchy induction, including link-based approaches, parametric methods, and topic models. Nevertheless, most of these techniques treat topics as abstract probability distributions over terms, omitting the direct utilization of raw data; moreover, they often struggle to process datasets of significant scale. This paper addresses these limitations by employing a Bayesian topic model that operates directly on raw data, specifically utilizing the Power Law Distribution over Transformations (PLDA) $\cite{pla}$. PLDA offers multiple benefits, including its ability to process datasets consisting of millions of items (e.g., documents or web pages) and their interconnections, function as a nonparametric method, and enable the direct estimation of relevant statistics without relying on approximations. In this setting, clients train model components (nodes) and upload them to the server, which combines active nodes for inference queries via tensor addition. We demonstrate that any scheme relying on ciphertext approximation is susceptible to zero-knowledge attacks, allowing an adversary with decrypted approximations to retrain via federated gradient descent to produce a predictor revealing target labels. Furthermore, we reveal that attacks are more potent when label encoding permits multiple non-zero entries. We propose removing this vulnerability by ensuring approximate schemes provide at least $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda)$-likely $\ell_0$ approximation for encrypted data. Leveraging this constraint and the cryptographic primitives of SEWALK (Secure Two-Party Learning with Almost-Linear Cost, STOC 2023), we design $\mathsf{MLP}$- and $\mathsf{RNN}$>-based inference protocols with nearly linear complexity. Our \textbf{RNN} protocol achieves security under the learning with errors ($\mathsf{LWE}$) assumption for ciphertexts, whereas the \textbf{MLP} protocol is conditionally secure based on the hardness of distinguishing real from noisy sketches. Additionally, our protocols support feature dimensionality growth beyond scheme approximations and allow deeper network depths by utilizing more active nodes. In terms of efficiency, our protocols leverage \textit{hardcode}, achieving faster runtime than competing methods for networks of all sizes and depths. For a specific network, our protocols are approximately $2.5\times$ faster when handling features with up to $10^4$ dimensions and provide up to $100\times$ improvement for smaller feature sets. Similarly, for networks with roughly $10^3$ active nodes, our protocols outperform schemes relying on tighter approximations. These results enable practical deployment, confirming that our protocols can process queries lasting a few milliseconds for networks with up to $10^5$ active nodes using $\approx 128 \times 128$-bit keys. Additionally, we demonstrate how to remove scheme dependence through sublinear preprocessing. Finally, we note that $\mathsf{MLP}$ protocols can be adapted for networks with non-differentiable ReLU activations.

While the atomic mass of neutral comets can be determined by tracking the motion of their atmospheric gas via spectroscopy, the mass of cometary cations remains uncertain, hindering a complete understanding of cometary volatile inventory through mass balance. Notably, the presence of these CO+ ions was directly confirmed. Consequently, the mass of CO molecular gas released by comets can be derived from the drift velocity of C+ ions. Given a known mass of CO, other common cometary molecules such as CO2, H2O, and H2CO can also be estimated by measuring the velocities of their respective atomic ions. However, unlike CO+, the ions of CO2, H2O, and H2CO do not accumulate around comets; instead, they flow outward into the interstellar medium. We address the problem of predicting molecular properties within a framework that supports retrospective ensemble methods. These techniques allow a collection of models, potentially trained on datasets with varying levels of label noise, to predict molecular properties or chemical reactions. Our primary objective is to develop reliable predictors for drug-drug interactions, a complex task due to the high prevalence of noise in available interaction data. To achieve this, we train ensemble methods that utilize auxiliary labeled and unlabeled information. Specifically, we introduce a model that effectively harnesses such data, enabling the prediction of drug-side effects and drug-drug interactions, as well as intrinsic properties of individual molecules. These capabilities are essential for identifying polypharmacy risks and creating combination therapies. We assess performance across multiple benchmarks, addressing both absolute prediction accuracy and the ranking of unlabeled molecules. Our results indicate that these ensemble methods significantly surpass state-of-the-art single-model approaches, improving absolute performance by up to 15%, decreasing residual noise by up to 2-fold, and yielding up to a 3-fold reduction in a loss function tailored for retrospective ensemble evaluation.

Drawing on North Carolina court data from 1994 to 2009, this study assesses whether mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation reduces the probability of future re-offending. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis compares probationers ordered to undergo treatment against those who were not. The findings indicate that requiring treatment lowers the three-year recidivism rate by 5.6 percentage points, representing a 17 percent reduction. The impact is strongest in preventing future violent and property crimes, with effects intensifying over time following conviction. Furthermore, a cost-benefit analysis demonstrates that the reduction in crime generated by the treatment exceeds the expenses associated with providing it.

Recent advances have made modeling human language a top priority for the AI community. While deep learning techniques have yielded impressive results in supervised machine translation, they depend entirely on large annotated datasets, a hurdle that limits the training of effective models for low-resource languages. Although recent efforts have been made to pretrain language models on unlabeled text, these models often struggle to translate low-resource languages accurately because they are trained on data from high-resource languages. In this study, we investigate leveraging multilingual pretrained models for low-resource machine translation. Our experiments demonstrate that even when trained exclusively on unlabeled data, these multilingual models achieve superior performance in low-resource translation tasks compared to models trained only on annotated datasets. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of the strengths and limitations of our approach, offering insights into how these models acquire knowledge of language and translation.

Evaluating the generalization capabilities of pretrained language models (PLMs) remains a significant challenge, as standard benchmarks are often skewed toward resources abundant in English. To address this, we introduce a framework that assesses generalization by measuring a PLM's pretraining efficiency across languages with varying data availability. Additionally, we analyze cross-lingual knowledge transfer by testing in-domain and few-shot few-shot adaptation capabilities. Our findings indicate that while English-dominated models generally generalize better to languages with more training data, they fail to accurately predict performance in low-data languages. We also observe that pretrained models often inherit biases from their training data, leading to unfair advantages for cognates and related morphemes, which creates both challenges and opportunities for knowledge transfer. Finally, we offer insights into enhancing cross-lingual pretrained language modeling.

This includes enhancing the Level 1 trigger system, which relies on calorimeter data, by implementing a new Feature EXtractor (FEX) architecture capable of identifying simple local features within small input regions of interest (RIOs). Originally, each FEX was simple, functioning only as a linear perceptron trained to maximize acceptance for signal events while minimizing background. This document re-examines the FEX design using a larger dataset and explores extending its functionality as a feature extractor followed by more sophisticated downstream classifiers. Furthermore, based on post-legacy analysis, we propose enhancing the FEX by incorporating a dropout layer and determining its optimal number through posterior analysis. These improvements yielded a 7% reduction in false rejection on the signal and a 5% reduction on the background using a dataset 10 times larger than that used in the post-legacy study. These results reinforce the need for a non-linear classifier in the second stage of the trigger system and support the specific hyper-parameter choices identified in the L1TDS. Beyond the standard ROs, we also analyzed full jet events to assess the system's potential for learning jet-like features directly. Similarly, when applying the FEX to jets pre-computed before forming full jets, the analysis confirmed a multi-dimensional output is preferable for the downstream classifier. These insights are vital for the final design of the FEX, as the ability to process full jets without relying on pre-computed features is a key requirement. Additionally, the analysis of full jets revealed that a linear model was sufficient, a discovery that was counter-intuitive given the complex findings from standard ROs. We attribute this to the lower dimensionality of jet data compared to full jets and the higher noise levels, which hindered the learning of complex features. Addressing these challenges will be crucial for the post-legacy analysis. We hope our analysis provides valuable insights for the final design of the trigger system. This metric captures the variety of local atomic arrangements as a continuous scale ranging from ordered to disordered states, defined relative to a reference crystal structure. We demonstrate this approach across three cases: (1) a single material where a continuous disorder gradient is induced by varying stoichiometry, (2) a single material where disorder arises from different cation occupancies at lattice sites, and (3) a multi-material dataset ordered by grain size. Furthermore, we show that chemical descriptors can map to a meaningful continuum of local structural disorder, enabling the identification of trends in both local environments and physical properties, including those spanning the order-to-disorder spectrum. Ultimately, our framework for quantifying and organizing disorder in solids will guide future experimental and computational studies, fostering a deeper understanding of how both macro- and microscale order dictates a material's properties. While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps for DLKT lack standardization, hindering fair comparisons and potentially biasing performance results. Second, current DLKT studies frequently evaluate only the last few interactions, neglecting scenarios where multiple predictions are assessed after several subsequent interactions. To resolve these issues, we introduce PyKT, a Python-based benchmark library designed to standardize evaluation across diverse preprocessing and modeling techniques. The PyKT framework comprises four core components: a standardized evaluation protocol, a collection of educational datasets, an extensive array of DLKT algorithms, and comprehensive experimental results. Our comparisons reveal that DLKT performance varies significantly with different preprocessing methods, highlighting PyKT's role in facilitating robust evaluations. Additionally, experimental findings indicate that DLKT models achieve higher accuracy than traditional statistical models only when the number of interactions exceeds approximately five per student. Finally, we observe that DLKT performance plateaus as interactions increase, suggesting that these models struggle to generalize to new students. The PyKT library is accessible at https://github.com/wy-song/PyKT.

# Introduction

Evaluating and comparing educational data mining systems is notoriously difficult compared to evaluations in other mining domains. This challenge stems from three main factors: (1) preprocessing techniques and evaluation metrics used in recent studies are inconsistent; (2) research questions are complex and rely on assumptions that complicate model evaluation; and (3) models often overfit, particularly when trained and tested on data from the same student. This report addresses these challenges by standardizing preprocessing methods and evaluation protocols for DLKT models through PyKT, providing a benchmark of results across various techniques on three datasets. These findings offer clear guidance for researchers developing new DLKT algorithms.

Recent years have seen intense activity in DLKT, driving up the performance bar and making it increasingly difficult for new models to achieve competitive results. We identify this as a critical issue in the field. To facilitate future progress, we provide insights into both preprocessing and modeling choices. Regarding preprocessing, we demonstrate that performance gains from specific features depend entirely on how the target variable is defined. Furthermore, we show that DLKT performance varies substantially across datasets, though the relative effectiveness of different feature preprocessing remains consistent. SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format. Finally, we request community input to guide future developments. Our evidence suggests that developing the proof format with a pragmatic approach is currently beneficial. However, adopting this strategy exclusively may not be sufficient for future progress. Therefore, we conclude by proposing that involving other communities in this process could be advantageous, as they share comparable objectives.

We examine the integration of recursive functions—specifically, features enabling veriT to interpret tuple structures like lists and strings—into the solver. This analysis includes a review of related prior work. We clarify how these functions operate within veriT, explain their encoding method, and provide examples. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of this integration for other aspects of the proof format. The veriT proof format supports user-defined inductive rules, which can be utilized to implement recursive functions. We illustrate this with a concrete example. Additionally, we show how to directly encode the interpretation of such functions to support checkpointing and continuation, although this method does not involve inductive rules. The benefits of preferring direct encoding over inductive rule-based approaches are illustrated through specific examples. Finally, we outline plans for future improvements to the format to support recursive functions more effectively.

While veriT primarily operates using QF_NRA (quantifier-free nonlinear real arithmetic), it also supports proofs for other logics, including QF_BV (quantifier-free bitvector) and SMT-LIB 2.0 arrays. This document details the representation of intermediate representations (IRs) within veriT for expressions, clauses, and formulas across these supported logics. Although the main veriT IR is based on QF_NRA, the system can process expressions, clauses, and formulas from QF_BV, QF_ARRAY, and extensions involving uninterpreted functions. We discuss various methods for translating these expressions into the primary IR and present a practical example. The document reviews the benefits and drawbacks of each method, with a focus on their relevance to proof generation, particularly regarding checkpointing and continuation features. We also explore how to represent IRs for other SMT-LIB 2.0 logics by

The \textit{FedBuff} algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) mitigates this issue by enabling asynchronous updates that tolerate staleness, thereby improving training scalability while maintaining privacy through secure aggregation. This paper revisits the \textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning, extending prior analysis by eliminating boundedness constraints on the gradient norm. It provides a theoretical examination of the algorithm's convergence rate under conditions of data heterogeneity, varying batch sizes, and communication delays. Furthermore, it introduces the \textit{FedBuff} variant, which supports a growing number of participating clients and allows for stochastic participation rates. Both theoretical findings and numerical experiments demonstrate that the asymptotic convergence analysis is conservative. The expanded understanding of convergence properties under heterogeneous and stochastic communication conditions can guide the design of more effective asynchronous federated algorithms. Overall, this work promotes the adoption of \textit{fedbuff} in practical deep learning applications.

Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Furthermore, when transferring to Czech, incorporating the intermediate-alphabet model leads to a substantial improvement, decreasing the final WER by 13% relative to a baseline that did not use the intermediate representation. Additionally, we demonstrate how our method can efficiently identify and flag translation errors within parallel text. These findings underscore the method's broader utility beyond ASR, potentially benefiting other sequence-to-sequence models that utilize parallel data, such as machine comprehension systems. We release our code at https://github.com/ctg-icm/ctg-kme/asr-transfer-e2e.

This paper introduces a novel, real-world Twitter dataset named "Twebera," which features diverse structural roles and multi-scale communities. We analyze various existing and recent proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embedding algorithms using the Twebera dataset. Our findings indicate that these embeddings effectively capture structural roles and communities within the tweet graph. However, our analysis of clustering results on embeddings derived from both the entire dataset and its subgraphs reveals that these techniques struggle to preserve multi-scale communities. These observations are reinforced by a visual inspection of the embeddings. The Twebera dataset is available for download alongside a link to its associated analysis.

We have long maintained that a comprehensive understanding of any system requires more than just identifying the roles of individual components; we must also examine how these components interact within specific contexts. These interactions are best represented as multi-scale communities. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for estimating where nodes belong to communities of varying scales. We introduce and methodology for evaluating node embedding algorithms that focuses on their ability to preserve these multi-scale communities. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that modern embedding techniques, including those designed to preserve structural roles, fail to capture multi-scale communities effectively. Consequently, any future algorithm aiming to represent the local structure of complex networks must be designed to preserve such multi-scale structures.

Twitter represents a vast repository of both proximal information and insights into user behavior, derived from accounts that post, retweet, like, and interact with messages from others. This study develops a node embedding technique specifically for Twitter that preserves not only local neighborhood structures but also identifies and encodes distinct community levels found within user interaction networks. These networks range from immediate neighbors to meso-scales and even global communities. We evaluate the effectiveness of these embeddings on real-world Twitter data concerning neighbor preservation and community structure. The results indicate that proposed embeddings successfully preserve local neighborhoods and some larger communities; however, they are less successful at capturing intermediate (meso-scale) community structures. These findings offer valuable feedback for enhancing future proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embedding algorithms.

Recent advancements in embedding techniques enable the representation of complex network structures as high-dimensional, sparse vectors, which can then be analyzed using standard data mining and machine learning methods. Evaluating the quality of these embeddings is crucial, especially when they are intended to facilitate specific downstream tasks. This work presents a systematic framework for assessing the effectiveness of existing and novel embedding algorithms

Dark energy constitutes approximately 68% of the current universe's energy budget, and the most viable candidates are scalar fields, such as the quintessence class. Treated as a perturbative effective field theory (EFT), scalar field dark energy faces constraints from various observational data points. While current limits on decay rates and annihilation rates for small black holes (specifically, $10^{12} < M_{BH} < 10^{24}$ grams) suggest that self-interactions must be minimal, we show that PBHs with masses $10^{24} < M_{BH} < 10^{30}$ grams could account for all dark matter if coupled to a quintessence field. These constraints are robust against variations in the matter source distribution function. Furthermore, we explore the connection between dark energy and the abundance of micro-PBHs, noting that certain quintessence models allow for a maximum dark matter density roughly ten times smaller than the critical value $\sim 10^{-9}$ grams/cm$^3$, provided the universe is near a critical point. Designed to address poor force measurements in SEAs resulting from elastic transmission nonlinearities, sensor noise, and deformation measurement errors, the paper first examines the limitations of traditional SEA force sensing methods. It then introduces the TFOB, which is synthesized based on closed-loop dynamics and real-time position data from the elastic transmission. A planar robotic system equipped with an SEA demonstrates the efficacy of this proposal. Notably, the system requires no force sensors, and the entire setup is cost-effective and easy to implement. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method significantly improves force tracking performance in a constant impedance control loop compared to conventional peak-hold valve control, with errors reduced to approximately 10% of those observed in a rigid transmission setup. Furthermore, the system achieves accurate force tracking even at very low levels. These findings confirm the high precision, robustness, and practicality of the proposed method, suggesting its value for enhancing force interaction performance in real-world applications. The source code for the transmission force estimator is accessible at: https://github.com/hj-lee/Force-Control-Using-TFOB.

The rapid advancement of robotics technology enables robots to perform diverse tasks, including manipulation, locomotion, and human assistance. Consequently, there is a growing demand for high precision force control to ensure the safety of human-robot interactions. While direct force sensors offer accuracy, they increase cost and reduce reliability due to susceptibility to noise. Therefore, elastic transmissions, specifically series elastic actuators (SEAs), are preferred as a cost-effective and robust alternative. An SEA consists of a motor, a rigid housing, an elastic element, a load, and elastic transmission sensors that measure elongation. However, accurate force measurement via these sensors remains challenging due to uncertainties in the elastic model, particularly when the load model is imperfect, precise position data is unavailable, or measurement noise is present. This work addresses force measurement accuracy in SEAs by comparing direct sensing with estimated forces using a transmission force observer (TFOB). The comparison evaluates error norms across various loads, loading directions, noise levels, and reflection locations. Results indicate that a TFOB designed with appropriate parameters can achieve measurement accuracy comparable to direct sensing. Conversely, a poorly tuned TFOB may yield more accurate readings than direct sensing under ideal conditions. The paper further provides design guidelines for implementing a high-accuracy TFOB.

Volcanic eruptions inject ash into the atmosphere, which impacts aviation, tourism, and agriculture. While visual evidence suggests that sudden stress releases cause particle ejections, the underlying physics remains unexplained. We constructed a numerical model of a volcanic vent to examine the flow dynamics of a multiphase air-ash system. Our focus is on the air-ash particle interface, specifically a particle raft analogous to an elastic sheet. By observing particle emissions, we observed that a sharp discontinuity in the velocity field causes a particle rupture, resulting in a stress release event. Similarly, a discontinuity in an air vortex causes a stress accumulation event. The ratio of the magnitude of the relaxation event to the stress accumulated at a specific point along the interface correlates with the intensity of the particle emission.

These fields transform under the fundamental representation of both the gauge SU(Nc) group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group, interacting via the most general quartic potential consistent with flavor and color symmetries. We analyze the resulting phase diagrams to identify low-temperature Higgs phases, characterizing their global and gauge symmetries and critical behaviors along various transition lines. Our methodology combines large-Nf and exact 3D simulations with scaling analyses necessary for extrapolating results to the continuum limit. In the Nf=2 case, we pinpoint several uncorrelated critical points, determining their leading phase-structure features and comparing them to prior research. Furthermore, our findings for Nf>2 reveal multiple critical points with distinct conformal data, signaling the existence of a previously unexplored window of Higgs phases. We also provide estimates for the conformal dimensions of the primary operators and their spins at these criticalities. Additional results include the specific heat of the critical theory, the number of flavors at the conformal window's closure, and the count of Goldstone modes within global symmetry-breaking phases. This study examines the influence of magnetic fields during gas-rich major mergers by conducting high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) and hydrodynamical (HD) simulations, tracking both field and gas dynamics. Our MHD simulations demonstrate that, unlike in HD scenarios where gas dissipates into the merger remnant, magnetic fields are amplified to very high levels in the central regions of merging galaxies. This amplification occurs due to the "direct compression" of gas against the stellar body, followed by the "weaving compression" of magnetic field lines within the high-density central gas. This process generates a potent "direct shock," which is strongly affected by magnetic pressure. Furthermore, in these magnetized major mergers, the " magnetic catastrophe"—previously observed in isolated gas-rich disks—transpires while the galaxies are still approaching one another. This event triggers a powerful "starburst," which is subsequently followed by a prolonged period of re-accumulation from the galaxies' outer regions. Ultimately, these findings indicate that the evolution of major mergers and the resulting elliptical galaxies is profoundly impacted by magnetic fields. The ultimate morphology of the merged galaxy is determined by the competition between the "direct shock" and " catastrophic collapse." We conclude that, depending on the specific merging scenario, this competition leads to significantly higher mass concentrations, more spherical shapes, and faster rotation velocities. These outcomes align well with the "major merger paradigm" and suggest that magnetic fields play a crucial role in shaping the morphology of major mergers and the subsequent evolution of elliptical galaxies. Finally, we propose that these effects may help explain why observed elliptical galaxies typically exhibit strong, large-scale magnetic fields. This research significantly advances our understanding of galaxy evolution by highlighting the vital role of magnetic fields in this process. The results may also help clarify the origin of magnetic fields in elliptical galaxies and provide potential explanations for the "radio luminosity" of these galaxies. Importantly, these findings indicate that magnetic fields can effectively prevent " core collapse" in major mergers of gas-rich disks. In summary, we confirm that magnetic fields can be a key factor in explaining why real-world major mergers exhibit high mass concentrations, sphericity, and rotation velocities. This underscores the necessity of incorporating magnetic field effects into models of major mergers to accurately determine the morphology and evolution of elliptical galaxies. We anticipate that future observations will support these conclusions.</think>

Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX).

First, we demonstrate that in any truthful bidding mechanism for two agents with over half of the valuations being zero, the resulting allocation is not EFX. Extending this result to all such mechanisms with an odd number of items is significantly more complex. To address this, we introduce the concept of weakly EFX— a valuation profile is weakly EFX if it is EFX when evaluated by any subset of agents holding strictly positive value. Furthermore, we establish that for any number of agents, there exists a procedure to obtain a weakly EFX equilibrium from a valuation profile where at least a third of all values are positive. searching for dark matter (DM), differing from the standard approach of using tonne-scale real-time detectors to observe nuclear recoils. Instead, this technique leverages small samples of naturally occurring, deep underground rocks, utilizing natural radioactive decay as an exposure mechanism. Over periods spanning decades to centuries, these samples would accumulate permanent, microscopic deformation events—such as displacements or displacements-induced luminescence—in their crystal structures caused by DM-nucleus scattering. Current experimental prototypes are anticipated within the next ten years, potentially using already synthesized mineral samples. Although current prototypes still face significant technical challenges compared to dark matter detectors operating at the LHC, projected next-generation paleo-detectors could achieve sensitivities that complement direct detection methods by propping up the nuclear recoil cross-section for dark matter masses between $100$ and $1000\,\mathrm{MeV}/c^2$. This review introduces the fundamental concepts of paleodetectors, reviews relevant physics and existing theoretical literature, examines potential target materials along with their readout technologies, outlines proposed prototype and future configurations, and estimates the sensitivity of these proposals. This work serves as a foundational reference for upcoming dark matter searches via paleodetection. Notably, several components of the proposed future paleodetectors could be constructed within a few years using materials and methods currently employed in active dark matter detectors. Furthermore, this research underscores the significant scientific potential of dark matter paleodetection in an era of shrinking parameter spaces for direct detection. As the field of paleodetectors is novel, we have adopted a pedagogical and educational tone throughout this review. We express gratitude to the entire dark matter community for their encouragement and support.

While definitive proof of such a signal in pulsar timing residuals remains absent, future acquisitions of enhanced and expanded datasets are anticipated to yield a statistically significant detection. Stochastic algorithms are employed to explore vast parameter spaces and derive inferences from this data. This study aims to eliminate biases stemming from sampler stochasticity during the inference phase. We evaluate various nested sampler configurations against the widely utilized Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, assessing both their performance on the pulsar timing array parameter space and their computational efficiency on identical datasets. We analyze a simplified parameter space mirroring the configuration in the Parker et al. (2015) study, which examined both stochastic signals and a pure noise model. Furthermore, we apply these methods to the full parameter space defined by Detar et al. (2019), consistent with the parameter space and data source from Detar et al. (2017). Although challenges regarding convergence and performance persist, our results indicate that nested samplers are viable for gravitational wave searches within pulsar timing arrays. They successfully recover parameter estimates consistent with those from MCMC analyses while avoiding the biases introduced by finite trajectories. For the full parameter space, nested samplers achieve parameter estimation performance comparable to, or surpassing, MCMC methods while requiring significantly less computational time. For the simplified space, we recommend configuring the nested sampler with 20 noise dimensions, 40 parameter dimensions, and 30 trajectories to achieve convergence within approximately 1 hour, though performance may vary depending on the specific nested sampler implementation. We explore the utility of 21-cm intensity mapping (IM) as a method for studying the evolution of radio sources up to redshift $z \sim 7$. Nevertheless, we show that even low-luminosity radio sources can contribute meaningfully to 21-cm IM signals. Leveraging the connection between radio and molecular CO luminosities, we link radio source evolution to star formation history (SFH) via supermassive star models. These models allow for the estimation of 21-cm IM signals from radio sources, which can be applied to interpret data from future IM surveys. while high-order interactions in many real-world complex systems are best represented by hypergraphs, these datasets are frequently released or analyzed only as projections featuring dyadic edges. To comprehend this problem, we first develop a theoretical framework to characterize its implications and worst-case scenarios. This analysis inspires the formulation of a new task: supervised hypergraph reconstruction, which involves recovering a real-world hypergraph from its projected graph by leveraging existing domain knowledge encoded in the edges.

To reconstruct hypergraphs efficiently, we analyze how edges can be categorized based on their presence within the projection and how this information influences recovery. Consequently, we propose a cost-aware hypergraph reconstruction approach that reconstructs probable edges with high accuracy while prioritizing the efficient recovery of edges that are critical for the hypergraph's overall application. To validate these methods, we validate them using a biological hypergraph representing protein interactions, which we then project into arbitrary -uniform and mixed-order (non-uniform) distributions. Our findings demonstrate that cost-aware reconstruction significantly outperforms baselines that rely solely on projected edges, achieving a $2.5\times$ improvement in reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, we show that the cost-aware approach is $2.1\times$ more efficient than methods that reconstruct every edge with equal precision. These results highlight that domain knowledge is essential for effective hypergraph reconstruction and indicate that similar principles can guide the analysis of real-world complex systems. Finally, to ensure transparency, we release our code at https://github.com/yj-625/HypergraphReconstruction.

Our findings demonstrate that the temporal coherence of the scattered field is governed by the average interatomic separation relative to the wavelength. In the high-contrast imaging of exoplanets, a coherent laser guide star (LGSt) projected onto a Adaptive Optics (AO) system enables the measurement and correction of wavefront distortions caused by atmospheric turbulence. This process, known as speckle nulling, involves suppressing the light originating from the guide star. We present a theoretical framework and conduct numerical simulations to show that when the angular separation between the target and the LGSt is small, the simulation outcomes diverge significantly from predictions made in the paraxial approximation. These findings are essential for determining the minimum angular separation required to apply a phase mask that exploits near-complete destructive interference to eliminate the LGSt speckle. While the paraxial approximation suggests near-total elimination, our analysis indicates that in the non-paraxial regime, the signal from a high-contrast exoplanet can be suppressed alongside the guide star. Ultimately, we suggest strategies to remove the planetary signal within the reconstructed spectral component.

Although the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NSE) is widely recognized as supporting soliton solutions, we demonstrate that the generalized NSE (GNSE) does not admit exact soliton solutions. Instead, we derive an analytical solution for the GNSE in the non-paraxial regime. We establish a mapping between the exact solution of the GNSE and a beam solution in the paraxial approximation, which exhibits vortex-like characteristics. These features are crucial for proposing a method to generate dark vortex solitons within a photorefractive crystal.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels, necessitating the adaptation to new environments with limited data. Consequently, offline multi-agent policy gradient methods must learn to adapt to these new settings while leveraging data of diverse quality levels. This paper investigates offline MARL problems involving multi-source datasets with differing quality levels and proposes a learning framework to solve them. Specifically, we develop a Quality-Aware Offline Multi-agent Policy Gradient (QA-OМПГ) algorithm. This algorithm learns an environment transition model to estimate dataset quality, then utilizes this information to combine loss functions from all sources when training policies via direct policy gradient. By weighting these losses according to their estimated quality, QA-OМПГ effectively adapts policies to target environments using data of varying qualities. Extensive experiments on multi-agent particle games demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art offline MARL baselines. The implementation is available online.

Image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) relies on real-time image acquisition and analysis to align the delivered radiation dose with the patient's actual anatomy. While online IGRT offers accuracy, it presents significant challenges, including motion uncertainty, radiation exposure to healthcare staff and patients, and extended processing times. Offline methods avoid these drawbacks but require robust image registration to handle inter-fraction variations caused by shifts in patient positioning and anatomical changes. Automatically analyzing multi-projection radiographs is particularly difficult due to low image quality and complex, non-linear intensity histograms. Our study evaluates several registration strategies, including similarity metrics like mutual information combined with optimization methods such as gradient descent, B-spline deformation, and hybrid approaches. Results indicate that similarity-only methods suffer from insufficient capture ranges, whereas optimization techniques often fail to achieve sufficient accuracy without hybrid methods. Finally, we explored deep learning solutions based on Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs), finding that these networks can perform prediction, segmentation, and classification on anatomical silhouettes extracted directly from radiographs with high precision. These findings suggest that deep learning techniques can enhance offline image guidance systems.

Although several studies have previously examined registration among radiographic, CT, and MR images, they often focus on a single modality pair. This work investigates various image registration methods across four combinations: CT-to-MR, CT-to-kV, CT-to MV, and kV/MV-to-2D. The investigation begins with an analysis of the intensity characteristics of these different radiographic and tomographic images. We evaluated multiple similarity measures and optimization strategies, starting with cross-correlation and concluding with deep learning approaches. These findings indicate that image registration performance varies significantly depending on the specific modality pair and can be enhanced by selecting appropriate similarity metrics.

conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen challenge to quantum theory by one year. Although initially met with skepticism, this concept later became a central element of the EPR paradox. The purpose of this brief report is to revisit that era through a specific lens: to illustrate how, merely one year after Einstein's proposal, Schrödinger not only fully comprehended the significance of this thought experiment but also advanced it with greater sophistication. To achieve this, the report utilizes the precise terminology and framework of that time, specifically the Heisenberg cut and the reduced density matrix, to convey the profundity of Schrödinger's insights. By highlighting this sequence of events, the account aims to restore proper historical context to a cornerstone of quantum theory that has recently garnered significant contemporary attention. Finally, the narrative concludes with a modern interpretation of the events described in this report.

Recent advancements have revived interest in the nonlocal implications of entanglement, suggesting that entangled states serve as a essential resource for executing Bell tests and securing quantum communication channels. This study investigates the degree of nonlocality inherent in local operations and classical communication (LOCC) separable states. We demonstrate that certain mixed separable states exhibit measurable nonlocality, stemming from the instantaneous wave function collapse across spacelike separated regions. This form of nonlocality, however, falls short of the stringent criteria established by Bell inequalities. Consequently, we characterize this specific type of nonlocality as "weak," distinguishing it from the strong nonlocality found in entangled states. This distinction clarifies why separable states can sustain the validity of local hidden variable models even when subjected to projective measurements. Furthermore, we show that the reduced density matrix of a subsystem within an entangled system undergoes sudden nonlocality—a phenomenon where nonlocality emerges suddenly under certain entanglement-breaking measurements, despite the global state remaining entangled. We contend that this phenomenon underscores the intense nonlocal character of the wave function collapse induced by entanglement. Finally, we contend that the term "nonlocality" is most appropriately reserved for entangled states, as they alone can violate local hidden variable inequalities, sustain contradictions within Einstein-locality frameworks, and enable the transmission of more than two orthogonal states without distortion.

By enabling stabilizer measurements through a single multi-qubit gate rather than multiple two-qubit gates, this approach reduces circuit depth. Using the toric code as a benchmark, this study compares two-qubit and five-qubit gates within parity-check circuits, focusing on trapped ion qubits controlled by Raman transitions where spontaneous photon scattering is the main error source. The findings demonstrate that a five-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen gate provides approximately a $40\%$ improvement in fault tolerance thresholds compared to two-qubit gates, highlighting the advantages of multi-qubit gates for QEC. This study investigates the advantages of using an five-qubit gate, specifically the $\Phi^5_G$ gate, for stabilizer measurement in quantum error correction (QEC). The motivation stems from the ability of multi-qubit gates to perform measurement operations with lower depths. The system under consideration is trapped ion qubits, where the interaction is generated by Raman transitions, and the analysis is tailored to this platform. The research is grounded in the concept of fault tolerance, comparing two systems that can encode a logical qubit: one utilizing two-qubit gates and the other employing a five-qubit $\Phi^5_G$ gate. The paper introduces the theory of fault tolerance, compares these two specific quantum systems, and discusses other multi-qubit gates relevant to various quantum platforms. Finally, the conclusions summarize the findings and suggest future research directions.

Our results demonstrate that these currents possess dissipative robustness, maintaining stability despite impurities and gauge field tilting within specific nonequilibrium states. Over the last few decades, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly advanced the automated discovery of new information, notably in scientific fields, by structuring existing data into the field of Data-Driven Science (DDS). By integrating large-scale, structured databases with intelligent tools, AI—particularly machine learning (ML)—enables researchers to streamline data management, accelerate the testing of hypotheses, and deepen their understanding of complex phenomena. While ML has been instrumental in this endeavor, it inherently involves uncertainties regarding both the processes and outcomes; this is especially critical in scientific discovery, as unaddressed ambiguities can lead to erroneous conclusions. To effectively manage these risks, it is essential to employ state-of-the-art explainable AI (XAI) techniques alongside traditional ML methods. This paper introduces DeepDash, an extensible framework designed to facilitate scientific discovery through ML while enabling real-time, customizable explanations of deep learning models. Although specifically developed for DDS, DeepDash is also applicable to broader AI domains. We demonstrate its utility in astronomical applications and release the system openly to support various AI-based scientific investigations.

This study tackles the challenge of generating safe CAV trajectories in such environments, with a specific focus on preventing rear-end collisions when preceding HDVs approach yellow or red signal phases. We introduce a predictive control framework that utilizes a recursive filter to estimate the driver behavior of leading HDVs. Based on these estimates, we develop a CAV control algorithm capable of initiating a protective stop when the predecessor's arrival time at the stop line becomes uncertain following a phase change. The proposed strategy is implemented in a macroscopic simulation of an urban intersection, where real-time access to live video feeds enables automated detection and tracking of a specific target vehicle. Simulation results confirm the practical applicability of our approach, effectively avoiding a potential crash during the redout period of a changing signal. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's capability to manage uncertainties regarding both the density of mixed traffic and the variability in driver behaviors. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research.

a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis. Despite their popularity, their internal workings remain largely mysterious, hindering effective error analysis and model improvement. While prior research has examined random LSTMs, LSTMs initialized with fixed parameters—and widely adopted in practice—have received minimal attention. This paper introduces a statistical analysis framework for fixed-initialized LSTMs, facilitating the estimation of memory and gate probabilities. We demonstrate that these networks inherently bias toward specific gate configurations, which aligns with design choices made by the Google team. Furthermore, we show that memory bias degrades performance on tasks requiring long-term dependencies, whereas increased memory bias benefits the next token prediction task. Conversely, gate bias is detrimental to both tasks. These findings offer guidance for balancing bias and variance, which can be leveraged to enhance fixed-initialized LSTM performance. We include code for reproducing all experiments provided in the supplementary materials, available as a public repository.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a popular architecture for processing sequences. Although they are frequently trained with fixed initializations, their behavior under these conditions remains poorly understood compared to randomly initialized models. We analyze LSTMs with deterministic initializations by focusing on the asymptotic limit of vanishingly small time steps. This analysis reveals that the network's statistical behavior is governed by the decay rates of memory correlations. We validate these findings against standard benchmarks: language modeling and translation. Our insights into the strengths and limitations of fixed-initialized LSTMs guide initial design choices and suggest avenues for creating more powerful models.

We propose utilizing dropout with non-i.i.d mask initializations to encode positional information within sequential data. Unlike traditional random dropout, this method requires no additional learnable parameters. When combined with dropout using random mask initializations, it yields a class of positional encoding initializations that surpasses both zero and sinusoidal encodings on long-sequence translation tasks. Furthermore, integrating this positional encoding with pretrained embeddings improves performance on both in-memory (short-term) and recurrence (long-term) prediction benchmarks for sequences up to length 65,536. Although parameter estimation indicates that longer sequences place a heavier load on the LSTM's long-term memory, these results suggest that the model performs effectively even with limited exposure to very long sequences during training.

However, this reliance on vast amounts of data hinders the deployment of NLP models in low-resource scenarios, where labeled text is scarce, particularly affecting languages outside the top 100 most common ones. Recent attempts to solve this problem by pretraining masked language models (MLMs) from scratch or with OOD domain data have yielded mixed results, likely because these approaches fail to exploit the structural properties inherent in NLP tasks. This paper introduces Pretrainthenmask (PTM), a unified framework that combines one-step in-domain pretraining with MLM masking to effectively learn language structure specifically for downstream tasks. In PTM, the model is initialized with a simple one-step in-domain pretraining module before being transferred to a target domain, whereas the subsequent MLM loss serves to refine the model by learning detailed language structures. Experimental results on low-resource cross-lingual classification and sentiment analysis demonstrate that PTM significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving improvements of up to 14.6% in low-resource cross-lingual classification and 9.1% in low-resource cross-lingual sentiment analysis. The code for this study is available online. In summary, our contributions are: (1) the observation that MLM alone is insufficient for effectively capturing language structure in low-resource settings, and (2) the development of the PTM framework, which successfully enhances both one-step and low-resource cross-lingual tasks. Model-space QITE (MSQITE) simultaneously diagonalizes the Hamiltonian within an expanded space comprising the ground state, excited states, and their corresponding Krylov subspaces. To achieve this, MSQITE applies multiple propagators derived from the Hamiltonian's spectral decomposition, with frequencies set by the energy gaps between these spaces. Crucially, the dimensions of the individual spaces and the intervening gaps serve as a variational structure that the MSQITE algorithm optimizes. Because these gaps directly influence the number and stability of simultaneously applied propagators, explicit expressions for the maximum applicable gaps and the count of simultaneously evolvable states are provided. Furthermore, to mitigate noise and errors inherent in Hamiltonian evaluations on quantum computers, a least-squares fitting function is employed to approximate the unitary propagator, enhancing the robustness and efficiency of the computation. We validate this approach using the transverse-field Hamiltonian as a test case, demonstrating results for both a ground state and an excited state. Expressions for MSQITE application to Fermionic systems and lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) are also discussed, with prospective bounds for these extensions estimated based on the system's spectral characteristics. Finally, we address the necessary conditions for MSQITE to converge to the Hamiltonian, noting that a primary source of error in this system-space method stems from the truncation of the Taylor series expansion of the propagator. Ideally, the sizes of the various spaces would be optimized automatically; however, we note that a fully automated optimization remains a challenge for future research. Overall, the proposed MSQITE method is anticipated to enable longer system-time evolution in quantum many-body simulations, thereby supporting more accurate extracts of excited states and their statistics. Additionally, we expect MSQITE to aid quantum algorithms that apply multiple time-evolution operators, including those leveraging spectral decomposition, quantum signal processing, and Hamiltonian quantum signal processing.

This paper introduces a new computational framework designed to examine market structures, surges, and their reaction to policy shifts. Methodologically, the framework consists of two main components: a computational supply-demand model capable of handling diverse policy instruments, and a event detection algorithm tailored for power markets. This algorithm pinpoints periods of heightened activity within price data, distinguishing themselves from normal operating conditions based on policy parameters. We demonstrate the application of this approach by investigating market structures and price dynamics before and after the implementation of minimum offer prices in Spain. Using a computational supply model, we calculate mark-ups and elasticities, revealing that wind curtailment occurs when wind offers meet these new price floors. Complementarily, computational event detection in Spanish electricity prices shows that the frequency of events increased following the introduction of the minimum offer price policy. Consequently, this framework is widely applicable for studying various policy instruments, offering insights into event frequencies and understanding where and why they occur. This includes analyzing the effect of price caps on event detection and utilizing load event detection to study backup power in data centers. Ultimately, the framework helps determine the consequences of policy modifications on events, a factor that is increasingly critical for planning in power and communications infrastructure. This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The newly formed NPSV was defined by a steepening thermal gradient near $78^\circ$N. Its hexagonal boundary suggests that the Rossby wave responsible for Saturn's persistent polar hexagon—previously thought to remain in the troposphere—can impact stratospheric temperatures roughly 300 km above the cloud tops. Additionally, we identified a compact region of elevated hydrocarbons at mid-northern latitudes ($70^\circ$--$75^\circ$N) at 2.5 $\mu$NHR, just before the northern polar vortex commenced forming. This feature suggests either an independent pollution source or the advection of material from an acyclic storm track. Comparing the vortices near the end of their formation phases reveals that the NPSV deepened via Rossby wave breaking, resulting in gradual thermal and compositional changes. In contrast, the South Polar Stratospheric Vortex (SPSV) exhibited abrupt step-function variations in both temperature and hydrocarbon concentrations. These observations indicate that the precursors for the SPSV's sudden compositional shifts remain unidentified, whereas the NPSV's composition evolved gradually from the start of its formation. Finally, the distinct morphological characteristics of these vortices suggest that the physical processes driving their formation and decay in the mid-streatosphere differ.

Consider the cubic Drude–Lorentz equation on a bounded domain $\Omega\subset \R^{d}$ ($d=1,2,3$) coupled with the Dirichlet boundary condition. Assuming $\overline{\Omega}$ contains the origin, the problem exhibits a bifurcating family of positive stationary solutions when a parameter is near a critical value. Traditional methods relying on bulk total energy or energy-Ehrlichsydov surface stress as selection criteria often fail to account for the influence of neighboring surfaces in system-specific equilibrium. Surface phenomena find numerous applications in catalysis, magnetic storage, and novel functional devices; however, deriving the optimal atomic surface model from bulk total energy alone is unsatisfactory, as critical energy-related surface observables are frequently determined by the order of multiple parameters rather than just energy. Surface screening using these energy-related surface observables is therefore essential for reliably identifying the optimal surface model without bias. For simple bulk materials, energy-derived surface stress can effectively evaluate surface candidate stability, but this metric is insufficient for predicting the ordering of surface adsorbates on bulk surfaces or for directly assessing the stability of superstructure surface candidates. Consequently, we have developed a surface screening method based on bulk total energy and energy-related surface observables. This approach successfully identifies the experimental surface model for Cu$_3$Au/(110) and resolves the optimal surface candidate for (110) Cu$_3$Au/Ag superlattices, a structure that cannot be predicted by bulk total energy alone. Surface screening via energy-related surface observables is therefore critical for reliably determining the stability of superstructure surface candidates on bulk surfaces.

While bulk total energy remains a crucial indicator for the stability of primitive surface candidates on bulk crystals, it is inadequate for evaluating superstructure surface candidates or those on interfaces and heterostructures. Although scattering processes involve complex light-matter coupling, many applications primarily rely on linear optics, often neglecting non-linear effects. However, the rising demand for ultra-short laser pulses enables access to powerful non-linear phenomena. This report examines the potential of applying non-linear optical techniques to spectroscopy. In this study, we employ a combined experimental and theoretical methodology to investigate the electronic topological characteristics of antimonene (Sb) monolayers with vacancies. While undoped group V Xenes typically possess an odd number of electrons per unit cell, suggesting a native magnetic state, experimental magnetometry of mechanically exfoliated antimonene confirms a non-magnetic ground state. To analyze topological properties, we perform both non-magnetic (undoped) and magnetic (25% Sb-doped) first-principles calculations to obtain the Hamiltonian, which we subsequently analyze using the $k \cdot p$ approximation. Our findings indicate that undoped antimonene acts as a semi-metal, whereas 25% Sb-doped regions correspond to a topological insulator phase. Finally, the ability to tune topological phases via doping and vacancies in 2D Xenes paves the way for creating heterostructures with other topological materials, such as 2D graphene, to explore more complex topological phenomena.

Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. This setup harnesses the combined influence of exchange bias, dipolar coupling within the magnetic layer, and superconductivity. We examine the system using a theoretical framework that integrates a Ginzburg-Landau description of the superconducting layer with micromagnetic micromodeling of the magnetic interface. Notably, we identify a novel phase characterized by localized superconducting vortices, where the vortex lattice spacing is determined by the geometry of the magnetic grating. We detail the emergence of this phase near the superconductor-normal metal interface and investigate its properties, including the impact of vortex dynamics on AC Josephson radiation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the external magnetic response near the interface retains a "imprint" of the periodicity from the underlying magnetic grating. Finally, we assess the viability of this spin-triplet valve for generating localized voltage signals in superconducting patterns, such as those found in Penrose tilings. These superconducting vortex patterns are shown to produce time-dependent voltage distributions with a complex, non-repeating spatial structure. This phenomenon arises from localized zero-energy modes on the vortex lattice and offers a macroscopic demonstration of a quantum quasicrystalline "scar" in the voltage distribution. Additionally, we establish a method to manipulate the superconducting state using a thermal gradient across the interface. This approach induces a vortex-antivortex pairing mechanism distinct from the native vortex pairing, effectively averaging the interfacial magnetic response in superconducting thin films. These novel phenomena in superconducting spin-valves could enable unconventional voltage patterns, including quantum scarred states and localized AC Josephson effects, to manifest on mesoscopic scales. These outcomes are highly relevant to the proposed kinetic inductance detector.

The pursuit of stable, localized pair-breaking modes with odd parity in superconductors is essential for observing Majorana zero-energy modes. We introduce a superconducting spin-triplet valve, where the onset of superconductivity is controlled by an adjacent magnetic metal layer. When the magnetic layer is structured into a valve-like configuration, its magnetic response to an external field exhibits a deep imprint from the field history, resulting in a highly non-equilibrium superconducting state. In a device where this valve is periodic, we show that the non-equilibrium state supports long-lived, localized spin-triplet modes.

science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses against one another based on their predictive performance within a specific model. Nevertheless, researchers often struggle to select an appropriate model, a difficulty known as the underdetermination problem. While hierarchical modeling is a recognized strategy to mitigate this issue, extending hierarchical Bayes factor methods remains challenging due to the difficulty of defining proper marginal likelihoods across a wide range of competing models. Furthermore, computational cost becomes a significant barrier when calculating marginal likelihoods for complex hierarchical frameworks.

This study addresses these challenges by utilizing the variational Bayes method to efficiently compute approximate marginal likelihoods for both non-hierarchical and simple hierarchical models, thereby enabling the calculation of Bayes factors between them. I demonstrate this approach with the competitive exclusion principle in ecology as a case study. The results indicate that even intricate hierarchical models are tractable using this technique. Additionally, the framework is implemented in Python at the link provided in the supplementary materials, serving as a resource for future applications.

Recent advancements in neuroscience have enabled the measurement of single-trial effects, prompting the evaluation of competing cognitive models through Bayesian hypothesis testing. However, comparing models via Bayes factors remains difficult when parameters are shared across multiple levels, as it requires calculating the marginal likelihood of a joint posterior distribution. While variational inference has long served as a computationally efficient alternative to exact marginal likelihood calculation, its application to Bayes factor model comparison within multi-level modeling has not been fully explored.

I introduce an approximate calculation method for Bayes factors using variational inference, testing it on various statistical models, including a recent multi-level drifting diffusion model. My implementation is available as a Python package at the link in the supplementary materials, which can facilitate model comparison in scenarios involving shared parameters.

In many scientific domains, data collection costs are significant, necessitating decisions between competing hypotheses before experiments begin. Bayes factors provide a robust method for quantifying evidence in favor of one hypothesis over another, serving as a utility to guide choices that maximize the expected utility of Bayesian model evidence. When these calculations are performed offline, they enable researchers to optimize experiments before data collection, a strategy termed sequential design that remains underutilized in cognitive science.

This research extends a previously developed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo approach for computing Bayes factors to encompass scenarios where parameters are shared across hypotheses, a common situation in cognitive science. The proposed framework is validated through both simulated and real experiments. Additionally, it enables researchers to employ sophisticated models with rich data structures while maintaining the ability to perform efficient sequential design

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between textual relations (discourse markers) and semantic relations. Although hand-designed textual feature extractors like MWE have been previously used for sentiment classification, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the connection between textual relations and semantic categories. We demonstrate that an automatic discourse marker inference model, despite being trained solely on textual relations without prior knowledge of semantic categories, performs comparably on classification tasks to classifiers designed specifically for predicted markers and even performs better than those trained on the explicit semantic labels present in the training data. Consequently, we argue that the capability to differentiate between various semantic categories can be learned from textual relations alone, rendering explicit knowledge of semantic categories unnecessary for learning the function of discourse markers in context. This finding suggests that human semantic knowledge is, to a significant extent, acquired in the same manner. Furthermore, we highlight the limited ability of current manual feature-based classifiers to predict sentiment on sentences containing new, previously unseen discourse markers, underscored by examples from our inferred set. Ultimately, we contend that machines can learn the function of these linguistic elements just as humans do.

Recent efforts have demonstrated that neural networks can discover the function of a word by analyzing how that word modifies the embeddings of the words it combines with, a capability termed "learned compositionalality." Artificial neural networks have achieved remarkable success in processing high-dimensional data for tasks such as classification and representation. However, a significant obstacle remains: existing training algorithms, including backpropagation, fail to match the biological plausibility found in the brain. To address this, we present a learning rule for a simple two-layer network inspired by models used for cortical functionality. Unlike standard backpropagation, our rule employs a local update mechanism that simultaneously computes gradients and performs training, thereby offering a more credible framework for training deep networks within a biological context. Extensive experiments confirm that our method is effective and superior to several existing approaches. The source code can be found at https://github.com/yqia0229/Teaching-Decoding.

We examine a learning rule within a hierarchical model composed of repeated layers of sparse Poisson populations, which serves as a probabilistic encoder for natural images. This rule accurately trains the network to represent these images while exhibiting key properties of visual cortex activity, such as the orientation selectivity of single cells and the orientation sensitivity of population vectors. When applied to a network where each layer consists of approximately 1000 non-interactive cells, our rule effectively trains a model designed to learn the orientation distribution of natural images, outperforming both the Bayesian inference algorithm and a spiking network based on the delay-gated unit rule in both accuracy and efficiency. We anticipate that our research will encourage the development of training algorithms for artificial neural networks that are both high-performing and biologically realistic. The source code is available at https://github.com/yqia0229/Teaching-Decoding.

If a quantum field theory maintains a continuous global symmetry group $G$, its nonperturbative dynamics can give rise to massive multiplets of stable or long-lived particles, which are critical for both current experiments and future high-energy colliders. However, when the symmetry group $G$ includes a non-Abelian chiral subgroup, the theory may admit stable massless multiplets, leading to singularities in correlation functions. This scenario poses a significant challenge to the standard Higgs mechanism, necessitating a reformulation of the decoupling of the confining scale from the symmetry-breaking scale, a situation that could be particularly relevant for quantum gravity. In this paper, we demonstrate that the consistency of the theory is ensured only if the global symmetry group $G$ is embedded within a larger unitary symmetry group. We provide two primary examples to support this claim: the conformal Witten percolation model and quantum chromodynamics (QCD) with three massless quark flavors. We contend that this embedding of symmetries is a fundamental characteristic of any consistent quantum field theory.
